1	<!-- What is established about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as it stands now, grouped by area: each entry the fact, its source and its test. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `FACTS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. -->
2	
3	# Facts on record
4	
5	## Execution model
6	
7	- F-7 **Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases, and only the compiled path runs the static type checker.** Walk switches the checker off, and no switch turns it on. So walk checks no static types of expressions: an ill-typed expression shows only when it runs, as a failed dispatch or as another run-time error, such as F-239's refusal of an `if` on a value that is not a `Boolean`. At load, walk refuses some ill-formed declarations: the `fortress-repo` skill's `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists them, with their evidence in F-29 (`comprises` clauses), F-142 (the Meet Rule for Functional Methods) and F-145 (uncovered abstract methods and `override`). The phases and where the two paths part: the skill's "How a program runs". Detail: `explorations/repo-internals.md`, "The two worlds".
8	- F-9 **`fortress typecheck` checks a program against the compiler's library, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, so it is no oracle for walk programs.** `Shell.java` calls `useCompilerLibraries()` for the command (row 69). P-12 has walk run the checker on its own programs after the switch-over, and walk cannot do so as it stands: it runs with type checking and the Scala checker off, the Java checker is gone (`compiler/StaticChecker.java:228-229`), and it has no case for the `CoercionInvocation` nodes that the checker inserts, by reading (row 833).
9	- F-11 **The code generator boxes every number, and boxing is the main representational cost of microGPT-shaped array code.** So a compiled `RR64` loop holds no `dadd` or `dmul` (the `fortress-repo` skill, "The compiled runtime"). In Java models of microGPT's three kernels, boxed elements cost 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]`. No such kernel compiles yet: the compiler prelude has no array type (row 305), and the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (P-37). In a hot compiled loop, escape analysis removes the temporary boxes, and one box per assignment to a mutable variable per iteration stays (F-301), as long as C2's inline depth reaches each box's constructor chain (F-302). Detail: `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 4; `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` section 4.
10	- F-12 **On the compiled path, the scalar `RR64` loop `bench1t` ran in 0.74 s in one session's measurement; the loop still pays for its generator, for boxing and for a transaction check at each use of its accumulator.** `bench1t` is `for i <- seq(1#20000000) do acc := acc 0.9999999 + 0.0000001 end` on a `var acc: RR64`, with both literals written in the loop. The time is the median of three loop-only runs at one thread (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, "The four timings"). Times taken in different sessions differ on this machine, so compare only times from one session. What the loop does, read in its bytecode (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` sections 4 and 5): the `seq` loop becomes the compiler prelude's `countedseqloop`, which runs the iterations in order by a recursive split over boxed indices, with a closure call per element; each value is boxed (F-11); and the accumulator is a volatile cell whose read and write each first call `BaseTask.inATransaction`, as for every mutable local (F-40, what a size costs at run time, whose sized loop pays the same check). Within the boxing and the cell, the report counts four allocations per iteration, an interface call to the native wrapper and the casts, the part that unboxed doubles and `double[]` would attack. No share of the 0.74 s is measured.
11	- F-17 **The bytecode cache can come up empty after a library order that reports exit 0.** Running the same commands again, one at a time, made the jars. The cause is not known. Check the five jars before a compiled run (the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`, "The library order"). Detail: `perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` section 1.
12	- F-18 **On the compiled path, the class loader makes the class of a generic instantiation at its first use, by rewriting the template's bytecode with ASM, and the rewriting only renames, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field.** The class is `InstantiatingClassloader`; the `fortress-repo` skill's "The compiled runtime" gives the mechanism. A size is part of the made class's name, as in `pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, the object `Box` at size 3 in the probe component `pNatMeth`. Inside the class, the size's descriptor is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` (F-129). A field of the template's type `T`, `LT;`, becomes `LFRR64;` in `Box⟦FRR64⟧`, and `[D` is no class name, so stamping alone keeps every number boxed (F-11). The team's direction for unboxing builds on this class per instantiation (the plan in `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java`; the loader's empty "expando" stub, `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`), but a loader that stamps an `RR64` instance with a `double[]` field, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), does not exist and is unmeasured. Walk instantiates generics in its own evaluator, not by classes. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/java.md` section 1; `coordinator/array-design.md` section 2 (probe 1); `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 3, way A4.
13	- F-19 **By the specification, the iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments of a call or an operator may run in parallel, and a program must assume that they do.** A `for` loop is sequential only if every generator is, as `seq(g)` or `sequential(g)` makes it. An implementation may also run them one after another (`evaluation/parallelism.tex:88-90`), so a program cannot count on parallel runs either. For the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator, each path starts a task only where it judges it worth it: walk by `TupleTask.worthSpawning`, which also governs a call's arguments, and the code generator by `ParallelismAnalyzer`. Compiled, a function call's arguments run in order (`CodeGen.evalArg`). A `for` loop over a range without `seq` runs by splitting the range into `do … also do … end` blocks. Under walk, every such block is a task, and walk's library splits down to single elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss`). Compiled, the first block runs in place, and each other block forks only where `BaseTask.forkIfProfitable` judges it worth it, as tuple elements do; the compiler prelude's `parloop` splits down to `FORTRESS_LOOP_CHUNK` elements, 1 by default. `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the pool of worker threads (the `fortress-repo` skill, "Parallelism and mutable state"). By grep, no program under `explorations/`, the model programs and the probes, writes `spawn`, which starts an explicit thread, or an `also do` block, so their parallelism comes only from loops, tuples and arguments. The revival's tests under `ProjectFortress/` write both. Source: `Specification/basic/expressions/for.tex:28-32`, `tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:58-59`, `evaluation/parallelism.tex:50-80`.
14	- F-20 **Sizes, the `nat` and `int` static parameters, are values at run time; they check shapes, and no optimization uses them (F-40, what a size costs at run time).** The compiled checker checks them (F-67), and a sized program loads and runs compiled (F-129). Under walk, `Vector` and `Matrix` take their sizes from an array built at run time: `f[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\])` takes `s` from `array[\RR64\](3)`, and overloads on `Vector` and `Matrix` dispatch by rank (row 214). The array-type syntax `T[n]` with a `nat` parameter does not unify with such an array, "Cannot unify … with ArrayType", where `T[3]` with a literal size does (row 23). Walk matches sizes at dispatch. A mismatch, such as a `DOT`, the library's inner product, of a 2×3 matrix by a 2×3 matrix, whose inner sizes differ, is a `ProgramError`, "Failed to find any matching overload", that no `catch` takes (row 254). Source: `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:96`.
15	- F-21 **The February 2011 Working Draft's bare `Nothing`, one object for every `T`, is accepted on neither path: the grammar refuses its `excludes` clause, and without that clause `T` is undefined.** The declaration is `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/convenience.tex:40`). Both paths stop at a syntax error at `excludes`, since an object has no `excludes` clause (measured: `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, E4). Without that clause, both report `T is undefined` at the `T` of the `extends` clause: a `where` clause on an object binds no type variable of its `extends` clause, as row 17 holds for a trait. Today's specification refuses the form in any case, by instantiation exclusion, and marks it "Not allowed" beside the parametric `Nothing[\T\]` that the interpreter's library writes (F-167). P-90 still calls the bare `Nothing` future work that waits for such `where` clauses, not tried before then. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-maybe/REPORT.md` section 5.
16	- F-22 **When a component's name differs from the api that it exports, neither path finds the component, for an exported function or variable alike.** The specification resolves an imported api to any component that exports it (`Specification/basic/components/overview.tex`). The tree looks only under the api's name, unless a user maps the api to its component by hand with `LinkShell`'s `alink` or `clink`. The linker's component repository looks this way (`Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`), so `fortress link` and walk print "Could not find an implementation for API … on path" before any code is generated. The code generator names a reference to an exported declaration after the api, and the declaring class after the component. The link step rewrites such a reference to the component only when the repository names it, so files compiled one by one, without `fortress link`, die with `NoClassDefFoundError`. The missing step is the repository's: finding the component that exports the api. The report names two repairs, neither built: the repository could search the source path for that component, or the code generator could emit api-named forwarders, for which three comments in `CodeGen.java` leave a place. Walk and `fortress link` need the first. Workaround: name the api after its component. Gated by the expected failure `compiler_tests/XXXExportVarRungXLinked.test` (row 320). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-export-var/REPORT.md`, "The measurement that separates them".
17	- F-23 **A comment placed after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span and of the unambiguous name the parser derives from it.** The parser's `createSpan` trims back over spaces only, and a declaration that ends in `end` is unaffected (row 359). So a comment-only library edit can change the syntax tree, and a before-and-after comparison of parse trees or diagnostics maps positions back first. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/REPORT.md` section 6, D1.
18	- F-24 **Under `walk`, a native can raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees.** It throws a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object, as `Int.overflow()` does for `IntegerOverflow` (F-132; row 347, fixed). A native bound to a helper of `nativeHelpers/` raises the library's own exception where the helper raises a class of the compiled prelude, such as `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero`, so `DIV`, `REM` and `MOD` by zero on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64` raise `DivisionByZero` (F-299, F-306, F-308, F-312). Any other Java exception of a native becomes a `ProgramError`, which no `catch` takes. Gated by the `overflows(...)` assertions of `tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss`, and for a helper by `tests/NativeHelperRaiseWalk.fss` and, for each of the five types, `tests/<type>DivisionByZeroWalk.fss` and `tests/<type>RemainderByZeroWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md` section 4.1.
19	- F-25 **On the compiled path, the class loader loads each class under the JDK's class-loading lock, so the first load of an instantiation's class is safe on four threads at once.** `InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` holds `getClassLoadingLock(name)` for the whole load, as the JDK's own `ClassLoader.loadClass` does. Without the lock, two threads that first loaded such classes at the same time could race, and the run died with a `NullPointerException` (row 417, fixed). The test `compiler_tests/FirstLoadThreadsRungG` calls the generic overload `f[\T\](v: Vt[\T\])` at eight instantiations, `Vt[\A1\]` to `Vt[\A8\]`, from a parallel `for` loop of 800 iterations. Observed: at four threads it failed 5 runs of 5 before the lock, and passed 5 of 5 after. It is one of the gate's atomic runs, which run each program at four threads (`gate.md`). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` sections 1 (the runs) and 12 (why this lock).
20	- F-26 **Under walk, when one of two applicable declarations has static parameters of its own, the call chooses on their declared domains where exactly one lies inside the other, not by the order in which they are written.** It builds P-45, the choice among overloads by declared parameter types, under walk. A declaration has static parameters of its own if it is a generic function or constructor, or a functional method with static parameters in a trait or object without any. Its declared domain, walk's symbolic instance, is its parameter types with each type parameter standing for itself under its bounds. Where neither declared domain lies inside the other, where each lies inside the other, or where neither declaration has static parameters of its own, walk compares the domains of the instances that the call makes. So a functional method of a generic trait or object is compared on its instance, and a generic dotted method is chosen by F-253 (a generic method at a dotted call, also chosen on declared domains). If the chosen declaration is generic and its instance takes an argument only by a conversion, walk converts the argument and dispatches the converted arguments again, so the most specific declaration for the converted values runs. In two cases walk keeps the chosen instance, with no second dispatch: an overloaded dotted method, and a position whose conversion `Coercions.coercionFor` does not find, such as a tuple converted element by element. Two generic overloads whose static parameters agree in name, kind and bounds share one symbolic instance, even if their `where` clauses differ; no test or library declaration has such a pair (row 478). Gated by `tests/DispatchDeclaredDomain.fss` and `DispatchConvertedAgain.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.1, 5.2 (the second dispatch) and 5.5 (the symbolic instance).
21	- F-27 **Walk's load check reads again two kinds of overload pair that its parameter-by-parameter check refuses, and accepts those that pass: a generic declaration beside a plain one, read on their declared domains, and two plain top-level functions, not methods, whose overlap other declarations cover through `comprises` clauses.** To test a cover, the check cuts the overlap of the two domains, position by position, into parts by the `comprises` clauses. Each combination of parts must lie inside the domain of one declaration without static parameters that lies below both. So several such declarations may together cover the overlap. A search that does not settle refuses. A generic declaration beside a plain one passes where one declared domain lies strictly inside the other and the inner one's return type lies below the outer one's. Where neither lies inside the other, the pair needs the same cover, or declared domains that exclude each other read whole (F-258, exclusion over the whole parameter type). Equal declared domains are refused. It builds under walk P-46, by which a conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits, and P-60, by which several declarations below both may cover a meet. <!-- What is established about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as it stands now, grouped by area: each entry the fact, its source and its test. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `FACTS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. -->

# Facts on record

## Execution model

- F-7 **Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases, and only the compiled path runs the static type checker.** Walk switches the checker off, and no switch turns it on. So walk checks no static types of expressions: an ill-typed expression shows only when it runs, as a failed dispatch or as another run-time error, such as F-239's refusal of an `if` on a value that is not a `Boolean`. At load, walk refuses some ill-formed declarations: the `fortress-repo` skill's `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists them, with their evidence in F-29 (`comprises` clauses), F-142 (the Meet Rule for Functional Methods) and F-145 (uncovered abstract methods and `override`). The phases and where the two paths part: the skill's "How a program runs". Detail: `explorations/repo-internals.md`, "The two worlds".
- F-9 **`fortress typecheck` checks a program against the compiler's library, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, so it is no oracle for walk programs.** `Shell.java` calls `useCompilerLibraries()` for the command (row 69). P-12 has walk run the checker on its own programs after the switch-over, and walk cannot do so as it stands: it runs with type checking and the Scala checker off, the Java checker is gone (`compiler/StaticChecker.java:228-229`), and it has no case for the `CoercionInvocation` nodes that the checker inserts, by reading (row 833).
- F-11 **The code generator boxes every number, and boxing is the main representational cost of microGPT-shaped array code.** So a compiled `RR64` loop holds no `dadd` or `dmul` (the `fortress-repo` skill, "The compiled runtime"). In Java models of microGPT's three kernels, boxed elements cost 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]`. No such kernel compiles yet: the compiler prelude has no array type (row 305), and the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (P-37). In a hot compiled loop, escape analysis removes the temporary boxes, and one box per assignment to a mutable variable per iteration stays (F-301), as long as C2's inline depth reaches each box's constructor chain (F-302). Detail: `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 4; `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` section 4.
- F-12 **On the compiled path, the scalar `RR64` loop `bench1t` ran in 0.74 s in one session's measurement; the loop still pays for its generator, for boxing and for a transaction check at each use of its accumulator.** `bench1t` is `for i <- seq(1#20000000) do acc := acc 0.9999999 + 0.0000001 end` on a `var acc: RR64`, with both literals written in the loop. The time is the median of three loop-only runs at one thread (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, "The four timings"). Times taken in different sessions differ on this machine, so compare only times from one session. What the loop does, read in its bytecode (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` sections 4 and 5): the `seq` loop becomes the compiler prelude's `countedseqloop`, which runs the iterations in order by a recursive split over boxed indices, with a closure call per element; each value is boxed (F-11); and the accumulator is a volatile cell whose read and write each first call `BaseTask.inATransaction`, as for every mutable local (F-40, what a size costs at run time, whose sized loop pays the same check). Within the boxing and the cell, the report counts four allocations per iteration, an interface call to the native wrapper and the casts, the part that unboxed doubles and `double[]` would attack. No share of the 0.74 s is measured.
- F-17 **The bytecode cache can come up empty after a library order that reports exit 0.** Running the same commands again, one at a time, made the jars. The cause is not known. Check the five jars before a compiled run (the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`, "The library order"). Detail: `perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-18 **On the compiled path, the class loader makes the class of a generic instantiation at its first use, by rewriting the template's bytecode with ASM, and the rewriting only renames, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field.** The class is `InstantiatingClassloader`; the `fortress-repo` skill's "The compiled runtime" gives the mechanism. A size is part of the made class's name, as in `pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, the object `Box` at size 3 in the probe component `pNatMeth`. Inside the class, the size's descriptor is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` (F-129). A field of the template's type `T`, `LT;`, becomes `LFRR64;` in `Box⟦FRR64⟧`, and `[D` is no class name, so stamping alone keeps every number boxed (F-11). The team's direction for unboxing builds on this class per instantiation (the plan in `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java`; the loader's empty "expando" stub, `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`), but a loader that stamps an `RR64` instance with a `double[]` field, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), does not exist and is unmeasured. Walk instantiates generics in its own evaluator, not by classes. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/java.md` section 1; `coordinator/array-design.md` section 2 (probe 1); `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 3, way A4.
- F-19 **By the specification, the iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments of a call or an operator may run in parallel, and a program must assume that they do.** A `for` loop is sequential only if every generator is, as `seq(g)` or `sequential(g)` makes it. An implementation may also run them one after another (`evaluation/parallelism.tex:88-90`), so a program cannot count on parallel runs either. For the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator, each path starts a task only where it judges it worth it: walk by `TupleTask.worthSpawning`, which also governs a call's arguments, and the code generator by `ParallelismAnalyzer`. Compiled, a function call's arguments run in order (`CodeGen.evalArg`). A `for` loop over a range without `seq` runs by splitting the range into `do … also do … end` blocks. Under walk, every such block is a task, and walk's library splits down to single elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss`). Compiled, the first block runs in place, and each other block forks only where `BaseTask.forkIfProfitable` judges it worth it, as tuple elements do; the compiler prelude's `parloop` splits down to `FORTRESS_LOOP_CHUNK` elements, 1 by default. `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the pool of worker threads (the `fortress-repo` skill, "Parallelism and mutable state"). By grep, no program under `explorations/`, the model programs and the probes, writes `spawn`, which starts an explicit thread, or an `also do` block, so their parallelism comes only from loops, tuples and arguments. The revival's tests under `ProjectFortress/` write both. Source: `Specification/basic/expressions/for.tex:28-32`, `tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:58-59`, `evaluation/parallelism.tex:50-80`.
- F-20 **Sizes, the `nat` and `int` static parameters, are values at run time; they check shapes, and no optimization uses them (F-40, what a size costs at run time).** The compiled checker checks them (F-67), and a sized program loads and runs compiled (F-129). Under walk, `Vector` and `Matrix` take their sizes from an array built at run time: `f[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\])` takes `s` from `array[\RR64\](3)`, and overloads on `Vector` and `Matrix` dispatch by rank (row 214). The array-type syntax `T[n]` with a `nat` parameter does not unify with such an array, "Cannot unify … with ArrayType", where `T[3]` with a literal size does (row 23). Walk matches sizes at dispatch. A mismatch, such as a `DOT`, the library's inner product, of a 2×3 matrix by a 2×3 matrix, whose inner sizes differ, is a `ProgramError`, "Failed to find any matching overload", that no `catch` takes (row 254). Source: `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:96`.
- F-21 **The February 2011 Working Draft's bare `Nothing`, one object for every `T`, is accepted on neither path: the grammar refuses its `excludes` clause, and without that clause `T` is undefined.** The declaration is `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/convenience.tex:40`). Both paths stop at a syntax error at `excludes`, since an object has no `excludes` clause (measured: `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, E4). Without that clause, both report `T is undefined` at the `T` of the `extends` clause: a `where` clause on an object binds no type variable of its `extends` clause, as row 17 holds for a trait. Today's specification refuses the form in any case, by instantiation exclusion, and marks it "Not allowed" beside the parametric `Nothing[\T\]` that the interpreter's library writes (F-167). P-90 still calls the bare `Nothing` future work that waits for such `where` clauses, not tried before then. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-maybe/REPORT.md` section 5.
- F-22 **When a component's name differs from the api that it exports, neither path finds the component, for an exported function or variable alike.** The specification resolves an imported api to any component that exports it (`Specification/basic/components/overview.tex`). The tree looks only under the api's name, unless a user maps the api to its component by hand with `LinkShell`'s `alink` or `clink`. The linker's component repository looks this way (`Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`), so `fortress link` and walk print "Could not find an implementation for API … on path" before any code is generated. The code generator names a reference to an exported declaration after the api, and the declaring class after the component. The link step rewrites such a reference to the component only when the repository names it, so files compiled one by one, without `fortress link`, die with `NoClassDefFoundError`. The missing step is the repository's: finding the component that exports the api. The report names two repairs, neither built: the repository could search the source path for that component, or the code generator could emit api-named forwarders, for which three comments in `CodeGen.java` leave a place. Walk and `fortress link` need the first. Workaround: name the api after its component. Gated by the expected failure `compiler_tests/XXXExportVarRungXLinked.test` (row 320). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-export-var/REPORT.md`, "The measurement that separates them".
- F-23 **A comment placed after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span and of the unambiguous name the parser derives from it.** The parser's `createSpan` trims back over spaces only, and a declaration that ends in `end` is unaffected (row 359). So a comment-only library edit can change the syntax tree, and a before-and-after comparison of parse trees or diagnostics maps positions back first. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/REPORT.md` section 6, D1.
- F-24 **Under `walk`, a native can raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees.** It throws a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object, as `Int.overflow()` does for `IntegerOverflow` (F-132; row 347, fixed). A native bound to a helper of `nativeHelpers/` raises the library's own exception where the helper raises a class of the compiled prelude, such as `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero`, so `DIV`, `REM` and `MOD` by zero on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64` raise `DivisionByZero` (F-299, F-306, F-308, F-312). Any other Java exception of a native becomes a `ProgramError`, which no `catch` takes. Gated by the `overflows(...)` assertions of `tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss`, and for a helper by `tests/NativeHelperRaiseWalk.fss` and, for each of the five types, `tests/<type>DivisionByZeroWalk.fss` and `tests/<type>RemainderByZeroWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md` section 4.1.
- F-25 **On the compiled path, the class loader loads each class under the JDK's class-loading lock, so the first load of an instantiation's class is safe on four threads at once.** `InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` holds `getClassLoadingLock(name)` for the whole load, as the JDK's own `ClassLoader.loadClass` does. Without the lock, two threads that first loaded such classes at the same time could race, and the run died with a `NullPointerException` (row 417, fixed). The test `compiler_tests/FirstLoadThreadsRungG` calls the generic overload `f[\T\](v: Vt[\T\])` at eight instantiations, `Vt[\A1\]` to `Vt[\A8\]`, from a parallel `for` loop of 800 iterations. Observed: at four threads it failed 5 runs of 5 before the lock, and passed 5 of 5 after. It is one of the gate's atomic runs, which run each program at four threads (`gate.md`). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` sections 1 (the runs) and 12 (why this lock).
- F-26 **Under walk, when one of two applicable declarations has static parameters of its own, the call chooses on their declared domains where exactly one lies inside the other, not by the order in which they are written.** It builds P-45, the choice among overloads by declared parameter types, under walk. A declaration has static parameters of its own if it is a generic function or constructor, or a functional method with static parameters in a trait or object without any. Its declared domain, walk's symbolic instance, is its parameter types with each type parameter standing for itself under its bounds. Where neither declared domain lies inside the other, where each lies inside the other, or where neither declaration has static parameters of its own, walk compares the domains of the instances that the call makes. So a functional method of a generic trait or object is compared on its instance, and a generic dotted method is chosen by F-253 (a generic method at a dotted call, also chosen on declared domains). If the chosen declaration is generic and its instance takes an argument only by a conversion, walk converts the argument and dispatches the converted arguments again, so the most specific declaration for the converted values runs. In two cases walk keeps the chosen instance, with no second dispatch: an overloaded dotted method, and a position whose conversion `Coercions.coercionFor` does not find, such as a tuple converted element by element. Two generic overloads whose static parameters agree in name, kind and bounds share one symbolic instance, even if their `where` clauses differ; no test or library declaration has such a pair (row 478). Gated by `tests/DispatchDeclaredDomain.fss` and `DispatchConvertedAgain.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.1, 5.2 (the second dispatch) and 5.5 (the symbolic instance).
- F-27 **Walk's load check reads again two kinds of overload pair that its parameter-by-parameter check refuses, and accepts those that pass: a generic declaration beside a plain one, read on their declared domains, and two plain top-level functions, not methods, whose overlap other declarations cover through `comprises` clauses.** To test a cover, the check cuts the overlap of the two domains, position by position, into parts by the `comprises` clauses. Each combination of parts must lie inside the domain of one declaration without static parameters that lies below both. So several such declarations may together cover the overlap. A search that does not settle refuses. A generic declaration beside a plain one passes where one declared domain lies strictly inside the other and the inner one's return type lies below the outer one's. Where neither lies inside the other, the pair needs the same cover, or declared domains that exclude each other read whole (F-258, exclusion over the whole parameter type). Equal declared domains are refused. The specification's text allows `...` in an api's clause, and an extender that the clause lists (`Specification/basic/traits.tex`, "Trait Declarations"). Only a draft note refuses the api's own declaration of an extender, and a release build leaves draft notes out. The team's `compiler_tests/XXX3q` and `XXX10p` pin the refusal, so a fix that skips it for a listed type turns them red. One differential on climb batch 7C's tree gave the same errors at the same sites with the memo off and on: 626 at the distance stage and 75 at the count stage. Not converted, as measured: a declared return (row 387), a coercion with its own static parameter (row 513), and an overloaded function's tuple parameter or a tuple-typed field (row 395). Not converted, by the code, and not measured: a varargs or keyword element of the specification's tuple coercion, and its arrow coercion. Gated by `tests/Coercion*RungC.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-interp-coercion/REPORT.md` sections 1, 5 and 9.
197	- F-129 **A size is carried at run time as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`, and a program whose sizes are known at compile time loads, dispatches and runs compiled, apart from the open cases below.** It builds P-41. Each size value, such as the 3 of `Vec[\3\]`, has one descriptor; in a run-time subtype test, it is a supertype only of an equal size. A size read as a value is a constant that the class loader replaces by the numeral. Closures and tasks capture a size as a free static parameter (F-135). A size made from a number known only at run time does not run compiled: `tests/NatReflectTest.fss` stops at load (row 307). Gated by `compiler_tests/NatRt*`. Also open on the compiled path: a `ZZ32Vector` passed to a generic constructor fails at load (row 408); a dispatched overload arm whose static parameter has a concrete generic bound stops the compile in its sized form and dies at load in its type form (row 413); an object that extends two instantiations of one trait, one at a static parameter, passes the checker and dies at load (row 414). Row 416 is walk's defect: walk refuses at load `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])`, which the compiled run dispatches, since walk's overloading check applies no exclusion of instantiations. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-size-runtime/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 9.
198	- F-130 **The specification's wrapping operators ∔, ∸ and ⨰ are declared in the interpreter's library, and the library bodies and team tests that meant to wrap use them.** It builds P-73. The compiler prelude's ∔ and ∸ saturate, and it declares no ⨰ (row 348). One library body uses the operators where wrapping is wrong, by reading, not run (row 700). `Random`'s `LinearCongruential` computes `(mult DOTTIMES widen(state)) DOTPLUS add` and only then takes `MOD modulus`. So it agrees with the true state only where no step overflows or where the modulus divides 2^width of its type `N`. The library builds it only with the modulus 2^48, where it is right. Gated by `tests/WrapOperatorsRungD.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-wrap-operators/REPORT.md` section 2; their users, `reviews/wrap-dependent-code.md`.
199	- F-131 **The one library's number tower is flat.** It builds P-43. `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR64`, `RR32` and `IntLiteral` are siblings under `Number`. `IntLiteral` is the type that the library declares for an integer numeral. The compiled checker gives a numeral that type; walk still gives it `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit (P-76). Each wider integer type converts from each narrower one, and `RR64` from a `ZZ32` and an `IntLiteral`; a `ZZ64` goes into `RR64` only when written out (P-74). `QQ` converts from the five integer types and `IntLiteral`, and `RR64` converts from `RR32` too (F-139). `NN32` does not yet convert into `RR64`: P-75 decides that it will. `Number` declares no `=`; each type declares one at each type it coerces from or into (F-324). Under walk, a big operator over a list of numerals, with no static argument on either, such as `SUM <|1, 2, 3|>`, finds no matching overload at run time (row 432), and an empty `SUM` over an additive group that is not a number dies (row 436). Gated by `tests/FlatTowerRungF.fss` for every type but `RR32` and `IntLiteral`: that none is another's subtype, their coercions and `=`. `RR32`'s place is gated with F-139, and `IntLiteral`'s with F-79. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-flat-tower/REPORT.md` sections 5 and 17.
200	- F-132 **Under `walk`, fixed-width integer arithmetic raises `IntegerOverflow` when the result does not fit, as the specification says.** It builds P-73. Every arithmetic operation on a fixed width whose result can leave its type raises it, `^`, `CHOOSE` and `LCM` included, and a program can catch it. Three kinds of operation raise nothing: the wrapping operators (F-130) and `narrow`, the written conversion of a `ZZ64` to `ZZ32` or an `NN64` to `NN32` (P-72), which keep the low bits; and the shifts `LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT`, which lose the bits shifted out (F-125). Gated by `tests/FixedWidthOverflowRungB.fss` (`+`, `-`, `DOT` (`·`), `DIV`, negation and absolute value, on the four fixed widths) and `tests/PowChooseLcmRungE.fss` (`^`, `CHOOSE` and `LCM`). The compiled path is outside this fact. Its known gaps: the compiler prelude's ranges raise `IntegerOverflow` where their bounds sum beyond `ZZ32` (row 453); and `^` saturates, throws an uncatchable Java exception or adds (rows 523 to 525). Its `CHOOSE` raises `IntegerOverflow` as walk's does (F-305). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-overflow-natives/REPORT.md` section 13; `compile-ladder/rung-size-range/REPORT.md` section 12.
201	- F-133 **The one library's scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` alone.** It builds P-77. In the interpreter's library, a range that reaches `ZZ32`'s minimum or maximum has the right size and elements, with no overflow, unless it is strided and a difference of its bounds leaves `ZZ32` (row 522, below). On the compiled path, the compiler library has no strided range (row 514), and its range `IN` and `=` are always `false` (rows 479, 481). When the compiled checker reads the one library, as every compiled program will after the switch-over, a `case` with no comparison operator compares by `=` where the specification gives ∈, so the clause never matches. This holds where the guard is typed by a type variable bounded by a `Contains` type (the library's trait of a membership `IN`, which ranges extend), or by a union of them (row 480); over the compiler library the checker picks ∈. Gated by `tests/RangeZZ32RungJ.fss`, `tests/RangeBoundsRungO.fss`, `tests/SeqRangeTopRungO.fss` and `tests/RangeEmptyHashRungO.fss`. Open under walk: a strided range whose elements fit, but a difference of whose bounds leaves `ZZ32`, raises `IntegerOverflow` at construction (row 522). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-ranges-zz32/REPORT.md` sections 4 and 10.
202	- F-134 **A typecase or catch clause's bound name is a local on the compiled path, so the compiled `cast[\T\]` matches a value of type `T`.** `cast[\ZZ32\](0)` still throws, because a numeral is not a `ZZ32`. Open: a name bound inside a clause's pattern (rows 340, 498), and a named clause or `catch` in a `do … also` arm that reads a captured variable (rows 497, 322). Gated by `compiler_tests/TypecaseBindRungG`, `CastBindRungG` and `library_tests/ClauseBindingRungB`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 10.
203	- F-135 **On the compiled path, a parallel task in a generic declaration is generic over its free static parameters.** These are the enclosing declaration's static parameters that the task uses. The code generator makes the task class generic over them, a template like a closure's class, which the class loader instantiates at the enclosing call's static arguments. So, in a generic method, the operands of an operator that the compiled path runs as parallel tasks, such as those of the concatenation `||`, run in such generic task classes. Walk makes no task classes. Gated by `compiler_tests/NatRtTask` and `NatRtMethBoth`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` section 1.
204	- F-136 **On the compiled path, a generic top-level function, as an arm of a template dispatcher, is called at the dispatcher's own static parameters, by position, where it has as many static parameters as the dispatcher and each of the dispatcher's is a type.** Otherwise, by reading of `OverloadSet`, the dispatcher still reads the arm's static arguments from the argument's run-time value, as before the change. This is not measured for a count that differs, or for a dispatcher with a `nat`, `int`, `bool` or `opr` parameter (F-45). The arm's own kinds are not checked, so an arm with a `nat` parameter at a dispatcher's type parameter is not guarded out (by reading, not measured). Where one arm is more specific than another but does not line up with the dispatcher position by position, the dispatcher tests both at the call's static arguments, not at static arguments read from the value. So the less specific arm can run: through `viaT[\T\](x: T) = f(x)`, a `Box` runs `f[\T\](x: T)`, not `f[\U\](x: Box[\U\])`, and the checker accepts such arms where their return types agree (row 499, two expected failures). Generic dotted methods (row 495), and a generic declaration beside a plain one reached through an argument of static type `Any` (row 496), still die with `ClassCastException`. They die on an arm's static parameter left unrewritten, or on `ZZ32`, which the run time spells `…runtimeValues|FZZ32` and static code `fortress|CompilerBuiltin%ZZ32`. For template dispatchers both are fixed (rows 493 and 494). Gated by `compiler_tests/Dispatch*ArmRungG`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` sections 7 and 9.
205	- F-137 **Under `walk`, a generic call's static arguments are inferred with coercion, by P-74's promotion, also for the declaration that an overloaded call chooses (P-46).** A lone type parameter is one that is the whole declared type of some argument and that no other argument fixes through a type such as `List[\T\]`. It takes the narrowest of its arguments' run-time types, their coercion targets and its bounds that admits every argument. So `ZZ32` with `ZZ64` gives `ZZ64`. `ZZ64` with `RR64` gives the declared bound, the only candidate that admits both, since a `ZZ64` goes into `RR64` only when written out (P-74). With no narrowest candidate, the parameter takes its bound where every argument is below the bound (F-141), and otherwise the arguments' join. Walk, which has no static types, promotes from the run-time types. So where a static type is wider than its value, the two paths instantiate differently (row 509). The rule does not reach these open defects: a big operator over a list of numerals with no static argument (row 432); a `nat` parameter used as a value at an `NN32` binding, refused at the binding (row 486); a static argument that only the call's result mentions, at a typed binding (row 510); and a varargs or tuple parameter over mixed widths (row 511). Nor does it reach, by inference and not measured, a numeral that fits `ZZ32` passed alone for a parameter whose bound a `ZZ32` neither extends nor coerces into, since walk reads such a numeral as a `ZZ32` (P-76). Gated by `tests/InferCoercionRungK.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 9.

## The harness and the gate

- F-97 **The ladder-regression stage's baseline is `compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/`.** The gate compiles and runs the files of its `pass-list.txt`, and compiles only the eighteen components of the two microGPT programs, which its `microgpt-phase.md` holds at the phase disambiguate. The gate's step 7 runs the stage (`gateRole` in `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`; the `fortress-repo` skill's `gate.md`, "The ladder regression").
- F-98 **The harness's `run_out_WIcontains` key is whitespace-insensitive containment.** It collapses runs of whitespace in both the output and the expected string, where `_WImatches` collapses them in the output only. A key that `generalTestFailed` does not know sets no check, so a misspelt key checks nothing. A `run_out` with no check falls to the default: the output contains `pass` or `PASS`. Source: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/tests/unit_tests/FileTests.java:155-188`, `:276-282`.
- F-99 **The gate's thread count is pinned in the build file for the two suites, not in the calling shell.** `build.xml`'s `fastTrack` macro, which runs `testFast`, and its `systemShard` macro, which runs `testSystem`, set `FORTRESS_THREADS=4` (P-125). Without the pin, the suites would take the caller's count: half the CPUs if it is unset, or 1 under `env.sh` (F-203). `fastTrack` also pins `JAVA_FLAGS` to `-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, because a compiled test's run step takes its heap and stacks from it. With `JAVA_FLAGS` unset, a compiled test's run step (`bin/run`) gives its threads the JVM's default 1 MB stacks, and at four threads `library_tests/TimingRungT` overflowed in 8 of 12 runs (row 640). Detail: `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/build-efficiency.md` section 6.
- F-100 **`ant compileAll` deletes the caches folders, `default_repository/caches` and `local_repository/caches`, the linker's untracked `global.map` with them, when the implementation changed, and keeps them otherwise.** It compares a folder's `implementation.stamp` with the new build's. After a deletion, `fortress run` dies with `NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32` until the library order refills the five library jars, in about two minutes (the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`). Two other things clear the caches: `ant cleanCache`, which deletes both folders whatever the stamp, and `Shell.resetRepository`, which empties the calling run's caches folder (`ProjectProperties.CACHES`), and which `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` call unless `fortress.junit.reset` is false, as `testFast` sets it. A `fortress compile` after a rebuild of the compiler does not clear them. The linker writes a missing `global.map` again, empty. Detail: `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/build-efficiency.md` section 2.
- F-101 **`harness-one.sh` keeps its Fortress cache between calls.** The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh`, and its cache is the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It reuses the cache while the built implementation and the Fortress sources on the source path are those that filled it. `COLD_CACHE=1` empties it first. Detail: `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/build-efficiency.md` sections 1 and 4.
- F-102 **An `XXX*.fss` in the interpreter corpus is a gated expected-failure test.** `SystemJUTest` marks a file of `ProjectFortress/tests/` whose name starts with `XXX` as one that must fail, and the suite goes red when it passes. Such a test needs a `.test` file only to name a refusal at load, as any program of `tests/` does (F-29: walk's load check and its `load_exception_contains` key). An `XXX` test that imports an api with its component, as `XXXImportImportCollision.fss` does, takes them from `ProjectFortress/test_library/`, so it needs no new api folder. The compiled corpora's rule differs (F-103). Source: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/tests/unit_tests/FileTests.java:780-782` and `:394-412`; the `fortress-repo` skill's `tests-writing.md`, "How `XXX` works".
- F-103 **The `XXX` expected-failure mechanism in `compiler_tests/` and `library_tests/` cannot express, in one `.test` file, a program that compiles and then fails at run time.** The `XXX` prefix of a `.test` file's name makes every command that the file drives a must-fail. So such a defect needs two `.test` files over one component: a plain-named file that drives `link`, and an `XXX` file that drives `run` (the `fortress-repo` skill's `tests-writing.md`, "Writing an `XXX` test"). A compile-stage failure needs one `XXX` compile test. An `XXX` compile test with a `compile_err_contains` key whose program compiles is red: "Saw wrong failure". Detail: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-tryatomic/REPORT.md`, "The measured defect, and its home".
- F-104 **A thrown `CompilerError` takes a third path through the test harness, the exception stream, keyed on the component that `tests=` names, with check keys `compile_exception_*`.** The harness checks three streams of a command: its output, its error output and a thrown exception. `Shell` does not catch a `CompilerError` from the code generator, such as a code-generator wall (a `sayWhat` call; the `fortress-repo` skill's `references/compiler.md`). So the harness reads it as an exception of the component that the `.test` file's `tests=` line names. If that component's name holds `XXX`, a link or compile exception is green whatever the `.test` file is called; only an unmet key of that command makes it red. A `compile_exception_contains` key pins the wall's text, so the test turns red when the wall goes away or changes. Detail: `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-2/REPAIR-review.md` section 2.
- F-105 **`testSystem`'s four shards are one suite split by sorted index, so per-shard counts are not comparable across a change to the interpreter corpus and only their sum is.** Shard i takes every file whose index in the sorted list is i modulo 4, so an added file moves every later one. `gate_compare` in `coordinator/tools/gate-functions.sh` sums the `system-<i>` rows before it compares. Detail: `compile-ladder/climb-batch-2/JUDGE-gate.md` section 1.
- F-106 **The native-wrapper generator wraps every method, static or instance, of a class that `import java` names, private ones too, but skips constructors, static initializers and every method with a Java `byte`, `short` or array type in its parameters or result. A wrapped method with a type that has no Fortress counterpart makes the generator refuse the whole import.** The generator writes the compiled path's Fortress wrappers for such a class. So a method of a `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers` class that a library component names in `import java` needs a signature that maps to Fortress, private or not, unless the generator skips it. A class that no `import java` names is not bound by this: `systemHelper.setFinalStatic(Field, Object)` does not map. Gap-ledger row 368 records the refusal. Evidence: observed when a private helper with a `Class<?>` parameter broke the rebuild (`compile-ladder/rung-default-rendering/REPORT.md`, "The repair round"); the skips read in `FortressMethodAdapter.visitMethod` and `SignatureParser.unsayable`.
- F-107 **Three heaps run the interpreter, and a gated test can pass at two of them and die at the third.** `bin/fortress` gives walk's JVM 256 MB unless `JAVA_FLAGS` is set (row 67: a 2M-element array exhausts it). The harness runs each walk test inside its JUnit JVM, at 768 MB (`junitMem` in `build.xml`). `env.sh` and the `fortress-repo` skill's setup lines set `JAVA_FLAGS` to 4 GB with 64 MB stacks. Measure a claim about a walk failure near a memory limit at 256 MB. A compiled run is not one of the three: `bin/fortress run` goes through `bin/run`, which gives 1536 MB unless `JAVA_FLAGS` is set, and `testFast` gives a compiled test's run step 4 GB with 64 MB stacks (F-99). Evidence: observed: before its repair, `IntSemanticsRungI.fss` passed at 4 GB and at 768 MB and died with `OutOfMemoryError` at 256 MB (`compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md` sections 3 and 4.4).
- F-108 **The interpreter's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that is not a property of the program.** Without the flags below, as `bin/fortress` and the suites run walk, the order varies from run to run. With three JVM flags set, `-XX:+UseSerialGC -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=1`, the order is fixed for a given library, and a library edit can flip it. The three were always set together, so which of them fixes the order is not known. The harness reads only that the `XXX` test fails, not the order. If an output comparison sees the order move, with the test's verdict unchanged, the move goes in row 430, which records this order, and does not stop the batch (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "Reserved points and repairs"). Evidence: observed: `compile-ladder/rung-wrap-operators/JUDGE.md` sections 3 to 5.
- F-109 **Two gated walk tests are refused by the compiler until the switch-over, since they need spellings that the compiler prelude lacks.** `tests/CoercionRedispatchRungC.fss` writes `SUM[\ZZ32\]`, an approved test line, and the prelude's `SUM` takes no static argument. `tests/expTest.fss` calls `asFloat`, which the prelude does not declare. Walk's gated runs need both spellings. Neither file is in the ladder regression's pass list. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-flat-tower/REPORT.md` section 15.
- F-111 **The checker-count and distance stages read only the compiler's phases, so an edit under `Specification/`, `Documentation/`, the test corpora, walk's evaluator and natives (`interpreter/evaluator/`, `interpreter/glue/`), or `explorations/` outside the stages' own folders cannot move their counts.** The stages' own folders are `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/` and `distance/`. Both stages run the compiled checker on the interpreter's library, not on the tests. The count stage calls `Shell.compilerPhases` with `PhaseOrder.compilerPhaseOrder`. The distance stage calls it with that list's first six phases, up to the type check. None of these phases is walk's own: walk's `OVERLOADREWRITE_FOR_INTERPRETER` is not among them, and walk's evaluator is not a phase. Compiler code that names walk's classes, such as `SimpleClassLoader`, was read and does not change what the checker reports. The library names walk's natives in strings: a glue class, which only walk resolves, or a helper of `nativeHelpers/`, which the stages read through the compiled path's rewrite at the parse as a call checked against the helper's Java signature (F-298, F-299). Evidence: read in the code, not measured: `checker-count/WorldFlip.java:25` and `:42`; `distance/DistanceMulti.java:40-43` and `distance/run.sh:127`; `compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java:125-147`.
- F-112 **The test corpora cite the specification by file and section, never by line.** A test names the heading of the section that it cites. In the library chapters, it names the trait or method entry too. A rung that renames or removes a cited section updates the citation in the same commit. One comment still cites a line, left as it was: `library_tests/IntLiteralArithRung7.fss:19` cites `Specification/library/apis/CompilerBuiltin.tex:374-383`, a generated file that is not in the tree (F-162: such a listing restates the library's own api files, so it cannot justify them). Source: the one-time strip of `.tex` line numbers, commit `dc0eee2fe`. The `fortress-repo` skill gives the rule to workers (`tests-writing.md`, "Names, comments, citations").
- F-113 **A harness run against another build's classes must point `FORTRESS_CACHES` at that build's caches as well as passing `-Dfortress.caches`.** A `.test` file's `run` step is a separate `bin/fortress run`, whose class path comes from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. Without it, the run fails "Could not load ... Resource not found". The run step runs no checker code, so the tree's own classes serve it. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-return-type-rule/REPORT.md` section 4; the `fortress-repo` skill's `worktrees.md`.
- F-114 **`ant testSpecData` runs 130 of the specification's 133 extracted examples under walk, as a gate step, and all 130 pass.** `SpecDataJUTest` runs `SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries` and `advanced`, not `library/`'s three, and `testFast` excludes it. It builds P-124. Five examples write no static argument on a generic big operator whose bound mentions its static parameter, and they pass only because walk leaves that parameter open (F-143; row 424, fixed). The count and the time: the last landed gate's `summary.txt`.
- F-203 **`explorations/experiment/env.sh` sets up a shell for the gate's runners, and sets `FORTRESS_HOME` from its own place in the tree.** It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` two folders above itself, replacing any value that the shell had (`env.sh:4`), so sourcing another tree's `env.sh` runs that tree's code. It also sets the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` and `JAVA_FLAGS`, and unsets `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`. It deletes a `/tmp/fortress*rats` parser folder only if nothing in it was written for an hour and every running `java` process started after its last write, so sourcing it does not break a live run. The compile ladder's drivers source it: `compile-ladder/run-ladder.sh` and its copy in `baseline-2026-09-19/`, and the two that the gate's ladder regression runs, `repair-r1-atomic-static/run-subset.sh` and `baseline-2026-09-19/microgpt-phase.sh`. Each of these sets its own `JAVA_FLAGS` after it. `experiment/setup.sh` sources it too. `microgpt-phase.sh` names the main tree's `env.sh` by its absolute path; the gate rewrites that path in its copy (the `fortress-repo` skill's `gate.md`, "The ladder regression"). The count stage's and the distance stage's `run.sh` do not source it: their headers tell the caller to source it first. A worker does not source it. It starts each Bash call with the `fortress-repo` skill's setup lines, which give the same settings (`build-and-caches.md`, "Setting up each call"). Evidence: read in the scripts; the deletion rule also in `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/build-efficiency.md` section 4.
- F-234 **A Fortress command that a worker types itself (`bin/fortress`, `harness-one.sh`, `junit.sh`, or `java` of a Fortress main class) starts a fresh JVM, and that start costs too little to pay for a resident compiler.** A resident compiler is a background JVM that serves Fortress commands, as Scala 2's `fsc` did. The suites start one JVM for each test class, and one for each of `testSystem`'s four shards, not one for each test: the harness runs each test file inside its JVM. Only a compiled test's run step and a `.sh` test, such as `tests/concurrentPrinting.sh`, start another process. In one measurement over 267 worker transcripts, the one-off commands took 17.5 % of the wall time of the workers' shell commands, and the suites, builds and stages 47.8 %. Over the workers' whole running time, the one-off commands took 6.4 % (11.6 % if every wait that the measurement could not tie to a run was theirs). Removing their JVM start-up would save at most 1.8 % (P-150: no resident compiler is built). What runs inside the suites and the stages was not measured. Detail: `coordinator/process-engineering/fresh-jvm-commands.md`, "Summary", "What a resident compiler could save, at most" and "Decisions not taken".
- F-283 **The 52 programs of the team's `DemoTests` reach their end under walk.** Run one at a time from `ProjectFortress/demos`, each exits 0 and prints no "fail", within a 600 s limit and on an empty input, with `wordcount2` run from the tree's root and `tennisRanking` given the three files of `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/tests/unit_tests/FileTests.java:806-815`. The demos run in no suite, so a batch that changes walk or its library runs them again (P-79). `Generator2Demo` draws its arrays by `random`, so a product of them can overflow in `PROD`, and one such `IntegerOverflow` stop in a run is not a regression. The compiled checker still refuses `trips.fss` (row 817). No gated test: the command is the driver in `compile-ladder/rung-team-demos/REPORT.md` section 13, and its output on the code that `4445d848b` committed is 'demos: 52 run, 52 reached their end'. Detail: the same report, section 3; `compile-ladder/climb-batch-27/REPAIR-review.md`, section 2.
- F-295 **The distance stage counts each api's own errors and crashes, so an error in an api that only a later target checks cannot hide.** `table.py` turns `#total` into `none:` for an api whose `@@TC API` line gives `errors=` above 0 and that printed no `@@SC` line of its own, naming it with its count, and turns an `@@TC API-CRASH` line into a `#crash` row of kind `api` (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/table.py:54`, `:61-67`, `:94-104`). It does not read the `@@TC COMPONENT-CRASH` lines that `tools/distance/shadow-patch.py:111-113` prints. Test: `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/test_classify.py`, `Readings`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-list-imports/REPORT.md`, sections 1 and 2.

- F-138 **Each integer type declares its own `MIN`, `MAX` and `MINMAX`, so under `walk` the family answers at the type that its arguments promote to.** It builds P-47. - F-139 **`RR32` is a sibling of `RR64` under `Number`, and `RR64` converts from it.** Nothing converts into `RR32`. Under `walk` two `RR32`s answer an `RR32`, and an `RR32` with an `RR64`, a float numeral or a `ZZ32` answers an `RR64`. A typed binding converts an `RR32`, but a declared return does not (row 387). On the compiled path the prelude's `RR32` has no `=` (row 528), and two `RR32`s answer an `RR64` (row 529). Gated by `tests/RR32SiblingRungV.fss`. - F-140 **A size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` is refused by the compiled checker when it is a literal or folded from literals, and by walk when it binds one; walk reads a size exactly.** It builds P-40. The checker refuses such a size outside its kind: 0 to 4294967295 for `nat`, and `ZZ32`'s range for `int`. Walk refuses it at run time, where it binds the size to a static parameter. Walk reads and computes a size exactly, with no wrap: it reads a size used as a value as a `ZZ32` up to 2^31-1 and as a `ZZ64` above. The checker types such a value `IntLiteral`. The compiled class loader checks no size that it computes at instantiation: `next[\nat k\]()`, which builds a `Box[\k + 1\]`, answers 4294967296 at `k = 4294967295` (gap-ledger row 675; F-222). Gated by `tests/NatBigSizeWalk` for walk's reading. The refusals are gated by `compiler_tests/XXXNatRangeChecker`, `XXXNatArithRangeChecker` and `NatRtBigSize`, and by `tests/XXXNatBeyondNN32Walk`, `XXXIntBeyondZZ32Walk`, `XXXIntBelowZZ32Walk`, `XXXNatArithProductWalk` and `XXXNatArithSumWalk`; each `XXX` test passes because its program is refused. Open under walk: an array of a static size from 2^31 to 2^32-1 dies with a raw `NegativeArraySizeException` (row 527). Also open, as notes on row 325 (a numeral outside a bounded integer type): on the compiled path a `nat` size above `ZZ32`'s range, used where a `ZZ32` is needed, as in a range, fails at run time, as a numeral beyond `ZZ32` does, and neither P-40 nor the specification says where such a size is refused; and under walk a `ZZ32`-declared return passes such a size on as a `ZZ64`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-size-range/REPORT.md` sections 6 and 12.
- F-141 **Under `walk`, a type parameter that nothing at a call fixes takes its declared bound, and a lone one with no narrowest candidate takes its bound where every argument is below it.** It builds P-48. A lone type parameter is one that is the whole declared type of some argument and that no other argument fixes (F-137); where some argument is not below its bound, it takes the arguments' join. A type parameter that the declared parameter types mention only in function domains, an odd number of arrows deep and never inside a static argument, as `T` in `g: T -> ZZ32`, is bounded by the arguments only from above. Where nothing bounds it from below, it takes the meet of its declared bound and the bounds that the arguments place on it. An F-bounded parameter stays open (F-143). A reduction or comprehension that writes no static argument fixes its big operator's parameter by the declared type of its value, else by its elements' join (F-228). That rule is the coordinator's call. Two more rules are defaults of the walk-instance rung's decision record. First, a parameter that only another fixed parameter's bound mentions takes that parameter's instance, not its own bound: `ap[\T, A extends T\](a: A)` gives `T` the type of `a` (D3, row 592). Second, a lone one whose bound mentions a static parameter has the arguments' supertypes among its candidates, and so takes their narrowest common supertype, never its bound (D5). Defects, each with an expected failure: two bounds that walk cannot meet (row 591); a bound only from above that mentions another static parameter, which keeps `Bottom` (walk's `BottomType`) (row 612); two upper bounds from two function arguments that walk cannot meet, which fail the call (row 616); a parameter that only the result of a function expression with no declared return type fixes, which takes `Bottom` (row 587); a generic passed over at dispatch when its arguments have several minimal common supertypes (row 589), whose repair changes which declaration runs, the curator's to decide. On lifting a function over the rows of a 64 × 16 matrix, the row slice `m[i,:]` took five times as long as a six-line user view (row 298). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-nan-comparison/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 2.
## The territory map

- F-179 **Tasks and transactions are implemented twice, in `interpreter/evaluator/` and in `runtimeSystem/`, independently.** A fix in one copy does not reach the other: row 302's fix is in the compiled copy only. Detail: `coordinator/map/modules-and-phases.md`, "B.11 The runtime".
- F-180 **`import java` is wired on walk through `ForeignComponentWrapper` and `ClosureMaker`, but four gaps stop it and no test uses it.** In a probe, six small Java patches closed the five gaps the tree then had, two of them for gap 4. A component with two declarations bound through `import java` then printed on walk what the compiled path prints. Gap 1, the type table, is closed on the tree: in walk's world the three-argument `NamingCzar.fortressTypeForForeignJavaType`, which walk's repository reaches for a written `import java` (`repository/GraphRepository.java:957`), reads a Java type as the one library's (`compiler/NamingCzar.java:369-372`; F-298), so a component with one such import now stops at gap 3, 'Non-top-level reference to imported …' (row 845). P-58 chose another way: a `builtinPrimitive("…")` body whose string names a static Java method in `nativeHelpers/`. Its compiled half is built, the rewrite of such a body into a call before the type checker (F-298); so is walk's half, a loader of such a method beside the glue classes (F-299). Two findings bear on any binding that both paths share. First, a helper raises a Fortress exception by naming a class of the compiled prelude, such as `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$IntegerOverflow`. Walk has no such class: its loader of a `builtinPrimitive` helper translates the raise into the library's exception (F-299), but through a written `import java` walk ends the run with a `FortressImplementationError`, unless the probe's patch for gap 5 (`gap5-helper-raise.patch`) translates the raise. Second, by reading, a helper whose parameters or results are compiled-path classes, such as `FZZ32Vector` or `CompilerBuiltin$IntLiteral`, cannot take walk's values. The probe's closure converts only Java's numbers, booleans, strings and `BigInteger`, and the helper classes, read with `javap`, have 50 such parameters or results; walk's loader refuses at load a binding whose declared type no Java type carries (F-299). Detail: `perf-probes/prelude/natives-shape.md` section 1 (the gaps and walk's half: "What each gap does to it", "Limits, by reading"); `perf-probes/prelude/natives-binding-probe.md` section 1 (the compiled half; its section 2 measures the `import java` form, which P-58 did not take); `compile-ladder/rung-natives-compiled/SKEPTIC.md`, "My programs, old against new".
- F-181 **The code generator compiles a function, method, object or trait declaration that carries a `where` clause in its own header, emitting nothing for the clause, and refuses every function or method with a contract (row 701).** The clause's constraints are the checker's. A trait's or object's contract does not reach the refusal: the disambiguator drops it (row 781); F-255 says how each path reads a `where` clause on an `extends` entry (row 774). Walk checks a function's `requires` clause and raises `CallerViolation`. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/compiler.md`, "What the compiled path cannot compile yet", gives the refusal and the constructs that the code generator has no case for; an array comprehension has no case either. A local function compiles as a closure, except in the four forms that F-320 names. A trait whose `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause size, of `NatParam`'s shape, compiles; a call that opens its value to the size fails verification (row 307). Where a generic type that such a clause lists gives a member's body, the code generator crashes first (row 812). A function's or method's own clause that introduces a `where`-clause variable compiles, and the compiled call dies with `NoClassDefFoundError` (row 867). Tests: `compiler_tests/WhereBoundFunctionCompiled`, `WhereBoundMethodCompiled`, `WhereBoundObjectCompiled`, `WhereBoundTraitMethodCompiled`, `ComprisesWhereFunctionalMethodCompiled`; `XXXFunctionContractCodeGeneration`; the `XXXNatOpenRun` pair; the `XXXWhereVariableCallCompiled` pair. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-codegen-where/REPORT.md`, sections 1, 2 and 5.
- F-182 **Both paths refuse a `type` alias, a `test` declaration of the form `test Id[gens] = Expr`, and a `property` declaration, in the index builder that both paths run (`scala_src/typechecker/IndexBuilder.scala:187-189`).** At top level, each stops its component with `** bug! Not yet implemented:` and the declaration's kind, such as `TestDecl`: the type alias in row 18, the `test` declaration in row 121, and the `property` declaration in row 122. Inside an object, a `property` declaration stops with an uncaught `java.lang.Error`, and a `test` declaration does not parse. The rows observe walk. On the compiled path, the type alias was observed to stop in the same way (`explorations/aliases-units-report.md:98-101`); the other two forms are by reading, from the shared index builder. A function with the `test` modifier is another form, and it runs under `fortress test` (row 120 records it working).
- F-183 **The compiled path's only array-like types are `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`, two hand-written Java classes declared only in its prelude and absent from the specification.** Each element access is boxed. No gated test makes or indexes a `ZZ32Vector` at run time. Gated tests make a `StringVector`, store two strings in it with `putValue` and assert its rendering (`compiler_tests/DefaultRenderRungS`), and read `args`, which is one (`Compiled2`). Passed to a generic object's constructor, either type fails at load: its descriptor class is `RTTIv`, where stamped code asks for `RTTIc`. Row 408 and `compiler_tests/XXXVecCtorLoad` hold this for a `ZZ32Vector`; the probe measured a `StringVector` too. A native helper cannot take a Java array, since the wrapper generator skips such methods. Detail: `compiler-probes/vectors/vectors.md` sections 1, 3 (step 9), 6 and 7.
- F-184 **A generic object referenced without its static arguments is a static error on the compiled path, and the checker never consults the expected type for it.** `b: Box[\ZZ32\] = Box` fails as an ill-formed type, and a bare `Empty` as an argument or a field's default as an internal error, `T is not in the kind env`. Walk fails on both. Writing the static argument avoids both. So a bare `Nothing` compiles only against the compiled prelude's own `Nothing` (row 331, P-90). Detail: `compiler-probes/maybe-inference/inference.md`.
- F-185 **The suites run two corpora ported by hand, and no test compares the two paths on one program.** `tests/` shares no file name with `compiler_tests/`, and its 11 names shared with `other_compiler_tests/` are other programs. `fortress.unittests.noopt=true` in `default_repository/configuration` turns off the bytecode optimizer's tests. `TransactionJUTest`'s multi-threaded half is commented out. By the map's one count, 121 `.fss` files in the suites' directories run in no test, and some directories are orphaned. Detail: `coordinator/map/test-coverage.md` sections A.1, A.4 and C.1.
