1	<!-- The curator's decisions about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as they stand now. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- P-48 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `POSITIONS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. How the curator and the coordinator work is that skill's, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. -->
2	
3	# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground
4	
5	## The goal
6	
7	- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.** The revival judges what the designers intended by the team's own sources: its Working Draft of February 2011, its texts on types and its code. `Specification/` holds the Working Draft as a living document: the revival revises it and states each change (P-95). The texts on types include the Types chapter of the specification's 2012 restart (P-25). In `Papers/`, they include the OOPSLA 2011 paper, Naden's 2012 write-up and the POPL 2019 paper with its technical report. P-26 says when code counts, and which source wins where two conflict. The revival does not redesign the language. A pure-Java microGPT is the baseline that compiled microGPT is measured against: the optimal result, the one to aim at.
8	- P-8 **Where the designers' own sources, the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations, give no answer, the curator decides by the goal, a compiled microGPT running fast, not by type-theoretic purity, and he stays true to the spirit of Fortress.** On the way to a compiled microGPT, he accepts the language's unfinished corners as they are, so that the work does not stall in theory. He has not read the specification, the papers on its type system or the library, and he takes the designers to have known more than he does.
9	- P-9 **The revival searches for the most readable expression of the microGPT algorithm.** C4 is the flat microGPT program (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), whose data layout follows Aaron Hsu's flat style of APL (P-29: C4 is not edited for speed before microGPT runs compiled). In C4, the polishing happens in the vocabulary, the array operations that the model's lines call: `FlatArrays.fss` beside C4, and what of it has moved into the standard library (P-27: what a program builds that a more mature library would hold goes into the library). P-87 holds the limit: the model's text is the notation, and a change to a model line is shown to the curator as a diff first. C4 is the target form of the APL microGPT program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`): the APL program is written so that each of its lines expands into the line that C4 writes by hand. C4 writes its hyperparameters as tuple bindings, such as `(nEmbd, blockSize, nHead, headDim, vocabSize, bosId) = (16, 16, 4, 4, 27, 26)`, the form to which the APL sub-language (P-10) expands a strand assignment, APL's binding of several names at once. The one-line form, declarations separated by semicolons such as `nEmbd = 16; blockSize = 16; ...`, is not used: the APL sub-language has no use for it.
10	- P-10 **The APL side quest is closed: its sub-language covers only what the APL microGPT program needs, and the parts of APL that it left unbuilt, tacit functions, characters and nested arrays, are not pursued.** The side quest built an APL sub-language in `explorations/apl/`: a DSL grammar that expands APL text into Fortress code over Fortress's native arrays, not an interpreter of APL. Its microGPT program, `explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`, stays in the microGPT check under walk (P-30: the check's limit of one minute; what the check runs: the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/interpreter.md`, "The model program").
11	- P-11 **The 2D notation is a gimmick: no work on it unless the curator asks.** The 2D notation is Fortify's rendering. Fortify (`Fortify/`, run by `bin/fortify` and `bin/fortick`) typesets Fortress source as mathematics in LaTeX, for the specification and the papers. Taken as programming syntax, such a rendering fixes one view of a computation, though the same mathematics can be written in many ways. APL, with one symbol for each transformation of the data, expresses a computation better. The rendering is presentation only, off the revival's path, and no argument in favour of Fortress. The verdict is on that typesetting only: the Unicode operators, such as `∑` and `×`, are the language's own syntax.
12	- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types; F-9 and F-290 say what walk and the library lack for that step. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).
13	
14	## History he knows (do not re-explain)
15	
16	- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.
17	- P-19 **The tree is not described as the third-party port's migration grafted onto the team's history.** The port is a third-party port of the tree to Java 9, which commit `8fe1daa8f` copied onto the team's last commit (the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/records.md`, "The repository's history"). By history, `main` descends from that commit. By content, most of the port's files are removed or redone, and only one piece of the port's code still runs: the `FTypeArrayList` fix for the JDK 8 `TreeSet` crash (F-165). Why: the tree is not built on the port, and the record must not lead anyone to think that it is. The files that still describe the tree so wait for the lineage cleanup; `coordinator/lineage.md`, "Files that still repeat it", lists them.
18	
19	## Decisions on record
20	
21	### The standard and the sources
22	
23	- P-25 **`Specification/` stays the standard, and the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart is cited beside it.** The restart is a new specification that the team began in 2012 and left unfinished (F-166). Where its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, a worker cites it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word. On the rules that the revival revises, such as the exclusion rule, the chapter is the designers' latest intent, which the goal is to finish, and `Specification/` is revised to follow it. Three of the chapter's passages bear on the specification; P-97 holds how the revision uses the first two. It names the exclusion rule "instantiation exclusion" and gives it in two parts: which instantiations of a generic exclude each other (`types.tick:355-360`), and, in its note, a rule on trait declarations (`:361-376`). The revised `Specification/` takes that form: the first part in its chapter on types, the second in its chapter on traits. It adds a `covariant` modifier for a trait's static parameters, which neither path implements and which is future work, off the path to microGPT (P-62). Third, it says that `Bottom` cannot be written in a program, as `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` already says of `BottomType`.
24	- P-26 **The team's later decision wins over its earlier one, in a text or in code, where the team made it the language's rule.** P-7 names the texts, from the Working Draft to the POPL 2019 paper. Code counts as a decision where the team built it alike for all its types, or stated its rule in a commit message, a comment or the checker. Code that its author called a stub, and code that works around a limit of the JVM or of the checker, serve only the implementation. The decision that they depart from stands. "Later" is the date of the team's work on the point at issue. The revival revises `Specification/` to follow a later decision. The one library follows it too, in place of the team's earlier code, such as the interpreter's library. Where two later decisions conflict, the goal decides (P-8). The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. Why: the Working Draft's early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run. So they learned what is feasible. They sought performance, and specialization was a must. Their later decisions include the exclusion rule, specialization and the number types of the compiler's prelude, siblings from 2009 to 2012 (P-43). The revival knows less than they did, so it does not second-guess them.
25	- P-27 **What a program builds that a more mature library would hold goes into the library, in the library's own way.** A program written on this library has a part that states its algorithm, and it can have a part that builds domain-independent machinery that the library lacks, as both microGPT programs do. A form of that second part goes into the standard library when, on reasonable judgment, it is not an extension of the program's own domain; a form that the library has for one number type, rank or sibling trait and lacks for another is the plainest case. Whoever writes it there first studies how the library does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern, such as its `excludes` clauses. This rule governs how the library is extended; it does not choose between two of the team's designs of the language (P-26).
26	- P-28 **Fleshing out the standard library is a very important task.** Its next layer is algebra: traits such as `Ring` and `Field`, which the library does not declare yet, and what machine learning's matrices and tensors need, so that the library's algebraic traits, such as `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`, reach them too. Why: the curator wants those matrices and tensors to have the mathematical rigour that the library's way of building its types promises. The work edits the standard library itself, in `Library/`, not a separate tree of the revival's own outside it (P-27, how the library is extended). It is parked off the path to microGPT compiled. Two matrix ideas of his wait beside it: square matrices of one size as a multiplicative ring, and diagonal matrices of one size as a ring whose product commutes.
27	- P-29 **Walk's speed is irrelevant to every judgement of Fortress's performance.** Walk is far slower than Python's interpreter (`explorations/microgpt-port.md`, "Step-0 results", a measurement of 2026-08-23). Fortress's performance is judged on the compiled path, once the compiler runs programs. So no performance decision rests on walk's timings. In particular, until microGPT runs compiled, C4, the flat microGPT program, is not edited for speed. The gate never runs microGPT's two programs, C4 and the APL-style program, because they run too long to be tests. Why: walk is the unoptimised path, as a debug build is in Swift, where performance is not judged either.
28	- P-30 **The check of microGPT under walk after a batch must take less than a minute.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. The minute is the curator's goal, for a check that runs only about two forward-and-backward passes of the model, not a full training, and compares the results with reference values. That is enough to show that the model's mathematics still works, and that the library's changes, such as those to the arrays, did not break it. A slower check is to him a waste of time. The commit stage of each batch, the step that lands its changes, runs the check as `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh`, the quick versions of microGPT's two programs at once, outside the gate.
29	- P-32 **The record's maps are kept current and used, so that nothing that the record holds is worked out again from scratch.** The maps are `FACTS.md`, `INDEX.md` and the territory map, `explorations/coordinator/map/`. The territory map surveys the repository down to where the team wrote the intent of each design. Part of that intent is written only in the papers under `Papers/`, not in the specification. So the map covers the papers too, and shows where to look up a design's intent. `INDEX.md` is read whole at the coordinator's boot, at the start of each session and after each compaction, and each worker's brief carries a mission briefing from the territory map, not the whole map. The territory map's surveys date from 2026-09-16 (its README), so a status or a line number in them can be stale.
30	- P-33 **The work toward microGPT compiled follows the phases, in the order that the curator approved.** These phases are steps of the work, not the compiler's phases, and they are numbered 3 to 6, after two earlier ones. Phase 3 ends when the compiled checker reports no error on the apis and components of the interpreter's library that the distance to the switch-over counts (F-53 defines the distance, says what it counts and holds its value). The library's other components are not part of phase 3: each is cleared before the first program that needs it, and at the latest before walk runs the checker (P-12), so `System` by the switch-over, since the compiler's tests need it (F-293); F-290 counts their errors. Phase 4, the switch-over: first the natives, the library's `builtinPrimitive` bindings made to run on the compiled path, then the compiled path reads the interpreter's library and the compiler's prelude is deleted; phase 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code generator's open gaps; phase 6, microGPT runs fast. Code-generator work goes on beside that order, under either library (P-37). Row 320, an api implemented by a component of another name does not link, is part of the switch-over's design.
31	
32	### The one library and the compiled checker
33	
34	- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. Why: the switch-over spares porting the interpreter's library into the compiler's; the revival develops the checker until it accepts that fuller library. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled; F-293 holds the compiler's fourth file, `CompilerSystem`). The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library takes a design of the prelude's where it is the team's later decision, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library.
35	- P-38 **The compiler prelude's own text is not repaired: its defects go with it at the switch-over.** A helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is fixed for the one library, and the prelude's value moves with it (F-313). Its `Maybe` block and its `REM` guard `if other = -1 then 0` stay as landed until the prelude is deleted, and their tests stay. Then the compiled tests respell its reversed wrapping and saturating operators (row 348), `ZZ64`'s compiled shift closes (row 381), and the specification's `shift` reaches the compiled path (row 383). `XXXShiftDeclRungI` is then promoted, and the switch-over batch finds the compiler tests that bind `shift`, a reserved name from then on.
36	- P-39 **Every batch's gate measures the checker count, and its total never turns the gate red.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. Its gate runs the gate's steps on their merged tree, and then the checker count, as step 8 (`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`); the gate of `fortress-repo`'s gate part has no such step. The checker count and the distance to the switch-over both count the compiled checker's errors on the interpreter's library. The count stops where the checker crashes or meets an error that it cannot get past; the distance counts every error, over all apis and components (F-53 defines both and holds their values). A rise of the count's total is reported and never fails a batch on its own. The count's stage can still turn the gate red on the faults that F-66 names. One is a checker crash that no rung of the batch listed in advance as expected, in the field `expectedCheckerCrash` of the batch's manifest, the part of the batch's script that declares each rung's task. Until the switch-over lands, every batch's gate also measures the distance, in a stage that only reports. Why: the count checks only the `FortressLibrary` component (F-53), so a native binding moved onto a helper in another component is checked by the distance alone, and P-58 has each moved binding checked from the step that moves it.
37	- P-40 **Sizes are checked, and a size that inference leaves unknown is an error only where it is used.** A size is a `nat` or `int` static parameter, such as the length of an array in its type. The compiled checker checks sizes, and refuses a size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` (F-140, the bound on both paths). Wherever the array design, the compiled path's design for arrays (P-85), creates a JVM array, it checks the length there, at run time, and refuses one over 2^31-1. A size that inference leaves unknown is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value. So a declaration may declare a size that none of its types uses, and pass. A call that cannot fix a size of the declaration that it would choose is refused, also inside an overload set, instead of passing over that declaration. In the rule that no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait, two instantiations differ when any static argument but an operator differs, so `Vec[\3\]` and `Vec[\4\]` are two; boolean arguments count too once the checker has boolean parameters. A size used as a number, as in the range `0#n`, converts to `ZZ32` where one is needed, as a numeral does. The 17 vector and matrix operators of the `FortressLibrary` api declare only the sizes that their types use, the change of `explorations/perf-probes/array-sites/e3-rebased.patch`. It finishes the team's own fix of 2008, which removed those sizes from the component only. The JVM length check waits for the array design; under walk such an array dies with a raw Java exception (row 527). The checker still passes over a declaration whose unfixed size occurs in its own parameter type (row 400). The checker compares no boolean arguments (row 406).
38	- P-41 **On the compiled path, a size static argument travels at run time as a descriptor object, as a type argument does.** A generic type's descriptor has a field for each of its static parameters that is not an operator. The team's code generator already emitted that field for a size, with nothing to put in it, and the size's descriptor fills it. A `where` constraint `I excludes Range[\I\]` was weighed and not taken: the team left such a constraint as an open question. `Index` stands beside `Any` and `Object`, outside `Object`: it is declared `trait Index extends Any`, which the desugaring and walk keep as written and the traits chapter names as an exception to the rule that every trait extends `Object`, so a tuple of indices is an `Index` and never an `Object`, and P-42's tuples stay out of `Object`, as the specification's `trait Tuple extends Any excludes { Object }` keeps them. `BoundedRange`, which cannot take the bound, since the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56), keeps its narrowed `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` under the method condition `where { I extends Index }`, the library's form for a member that applies at some instances only. Row 783: the subscript pair.
68	- P-157 **`Vector` and `Matrix` stay additive groups, and the overloading check's exclusion test reads the self type and the static parameters' bounds, so the arrays' scalar `+` and `-` stand beside the vectors' own.** The team's `Vector` and `Matrix` extend `AdditiveGroup`, and the library's generic block of `+`, `-`, `MIN` and `MAX` between an array and a scalar (P-88) stays beside them. With symbolic operators checked (P-155), the checker refused 8 such pairs, though no call fits both: a vector's own `+` takes two vectors, the block's `+` an array and a number, and arrays exclude numbers. So the exclusion test reads a self-typed trait's `self` as `C[\X\] & X`, the fact that P-146's extender rule guarantees, and its existential reduction reads the static parameters' bounds (P-152); specificity and the Return Type Rule keep the plain signatures. Why: it keeps both the team's library as written and the revival's block, and it was his first stance; taking vectors out of `AdditiveGroup` would have bent the team's design for a gap of the checker. Reading bounds is the POPL 2019 paper's own reduction. Probe A1 measured it (`perf-probes/self-type-exclusion/REPORT.md`): the 8 gone, nothing else moved.
69	- P-158 **A member that an api writes `abstract` is declared in the component that exports the api.** The component's trait or object declares each such member at the api's header, with a body or without one. The compiled export check refuses a component that leaves one out, and the checker then checks that each object defines it. Why: the compiler's prelude, the team's later work, restates each such member in the component without a body, and the team's export check enforces it; that way wins over the interpreter's library, written earlier for walk, which leaves some out. The specification's export rule is revised to ask the same (F-294). Without the declaration, a compiled client's call of the member dies with `NoSuchMethodError` (row 816).
70	- P-160 **The one library's `Number` opens: its `comprises` clause goes, so that a program may declare its own number type below `Number`.** The team's compiler prelude, the specification and the team's test `tests/extendNumber.fss` give `Number` no such clause. It went in two steps. First, walk reads the library's scalar `+` and `-` between an array and a number beside `AdditiveGroup`'s own operator, as the compiled checker does (P-152, the exclusion of two generic declarations; row 804, its walk half). Then the clause was removed from `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi` (F-324); the reflective QuickCheck generator got a way to generate a `Number`, `Number`'s `=` and `asFloat` left the trait (P-165), so that a program's own number type compares by its own `=` or by the library's fallback `=` through `SEQV`, and the tests that leaned on the clause were repaired. The clause stayed until the first step landed (F-318): without it, walk refused the library's array operators at load, and with them most programs. `AnyIntegral`'s clause stays (P-44). Why: the clause does no work for the compiled checker, whose count of errors in the one library and distance to the switch-over are 0 with it and without it; and a vector or matrix of a program's own complex numbers needs it gone, since the library bounds `Vector` and `Matrix` by `Number` and `MultiplicativeRing`.

<!-- The curator's decisions about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as they stand now. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- P-48 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `POSITIONS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. How the curator and the coordinator work is that skill's, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. -->

# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground

## The goal

- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.** The revival judges what the designers intended by the team's own sources: its Working Draft of February 2011, its texts on types and its code. `Specification/` holds the Working Draft as a living document: the revival revises it and states each change (P-95). The texts on types include the Types chapter of the specification's 2012 restart (P-25). In `Papers/`, they include the OOPSLA 2011 paper, Naden's 2012 write-up and the POPL 2019 paper with its technical report. P-26 says when code counts, and which source wins where two conflict. The revival does not redesign the language. A pure-Java microGPT is the baseline that compiled microGPT is measured against: the optimal result, the one to aim at.
- P-8 **Where the designers' own sources, the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations, give no answer, the curator decides by the goal, a compiled microGPT running fast, not by type-theoretic purity, and he stays true to the spirit of Fortress.** On the way to a compiled microGPT, he accepts the language's unfinished corners as they are, so that the work does not stall in theory. He has not read the specification, the papers on its type system or the library, and he takes the designers to have known more than he does.
- P-9 **The revival searches for the most readable expression of the microGPT algorithm.** C4 is the flat microGPT program (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), whose data layout follows Aaron Hsu's flat style of APL (P-29: C4 is not edited for speed before microGPT runs compiled). In C4, the polishing happens in the vocabulary, the array operations that the model's lines call: `FlatArrays.fss` beside C4, and what of it has moved into the standard library (P-27: what a program builds that a more mature library would hold goes into the library). P-87 holds the limit: the model's text is the notation, and a change to a model line is shown to the curator as a diff first. C4 is the target form of the APL microGPT program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`): the APL program is written so that each of its lines expands into the line that C4 writes by hand. C4 writes its hyperparameters as tuple bindings, such as `(nEmbd, blockSize, nHead, headDim, vocabSize, bosId) = (16, 16, 4, 4, 27, 26)`, the form to which the APL sub-language (P-10) expands a strand assignment, APL's binding of several names at once. The one-line form, declarations separated by semicolons such as `nEmbd = 16; blockSize = 16; ...`, is not used: the APL sub-language has no use for it.
- P-10 **The APL side quest is closed: its sub-language covers only what the APL microGPT program needs, and the parts of APL that it left unbuilt, tacit functions, characters and nested arrays, are not pursued.** The side quest built an APL sub-language in `explorations/apl/`: a DSL grammar that expands APL text into Fortress code over Fortress's native arrays, not an interpreter of APL. Its microGPT program, `explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`, stays in the microGPT check under walk (P-30: the check's limit of one minute; what the check runs: the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/interpreter.md`, "The model program").
- P-11 **The 2D notation is a gimmick: no work on it unless the curator asks.** The 2D notation is Fortify's rendering. Fortify (`Fortify/`, run by `bin/fortify` and `bin/fortick`) typesets Fortress source as mathematics in LaTeX, for the specification and the papers. Taken as programming syntax, such a rendering fixes one view of a computation, though the same mathematics can be written in many ways. APL, with one symbol for each transformation of the data, expresses a computation better. The rendering is presentation only, off the revival's path, and no argument in favour of Fortress. The verdict is on that typesetting only: the Unicode operators, such as `∑` and `×`, are the language's own syntax.
- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types; F-9 and F-290 say what walk and the library lack for that step. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).

## History he knows (do not re-explain)

- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.
- P-19 **The tree is not described as the third-party port's migration grafted onto the team's history.** The port is a third-party port of the tree to Java 9, which commit `8fe1daa8f` copied onto the team's last commit (the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/records.md`, "The repository's history"). By history, `main` descends from that commit. By content, most of the port's files are removed or redone, and only one piece of the port's code still runs: the `FTypeArrayList` fix for the JDK 8 `TreeSet` crash (F-165). Why: the tree is not built on the port, and the record must not lead anyone to think that it is. The files that still describe the tree so wait for the lineage cleanup; `coordinator/lineage.md`, "Files that still repeat it", lists them.

## Decisions on record

### The standard and the sources

- P-25 **`Specification/` stays the standard, and the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart is cited beside it.** The restart is a new specification that the team began in 2012 and left unfinished (F-166). Where its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, a worker cites it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word. On the rules that the revival revises, such as the exclusion rule, the chapter is the designers' latest intent, which the goal is to finish, and `Specification/` is revised to follow it. Three of the chapter's passages bear on the specification; P-97 holds how the revision uses the first two. It names the exclusion rule "instantiation exclusion" and gives it in two parts: which instantiations of a generic exclude each other (`types.tick:355-360`), and, in its note, a rule on trait declarations (`:361-376`). The revised `Specification/` takes that form: the first part in its chapter on types, the second in its chapter on traits. It adds a `covariant` modifier for a trait's static parameters, which neither path implements and which is future work, off the path to microGPT (P-62). Third, it says that `Bottom` cannot be written in a program, as `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` already says of `BottomType`.
- P-26 **The team's later decision wins over its earlier one, in a text or in code, where the team made it the language's rule.** P-7 names the texts, from the Working Draft to the POPL 2019 paper. Code counts as a decision where the team built it alike for all its types, or stated its rule in a commit message, a comment or the checker. Code that its author called a stub, and code that works around a limit of the JVM or of the checker, serve only the implementation. The decision that they depart from stands. "Later" is the date of the team's work on the point at issue. The revival revises `Specification/` to follow a later decision. The one library follows it too, in place of the team's earlier code, such as the interpreter's library. Where two later decisions conflict, the goal decides (P-8). The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. Why: the Working Draft's early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run. So they learned what is feasible. They sought performance, and specialization was a must. Their later decisions include the exclusion rule, specialization and the number types of the compiler's prelude, siblings from 2009 to 2012 (P-43). The revival knows less than they did, so it does not second-guess them.
- P-27 **What a program builds that a more mature library would hold goes into the library, in the library's own way.** A program written on this library has a part that states its algorithm, and it can have a part that builds domain-independent machinery that the library lacks, as both microGPT programs do. A form of that second part goes into the standard library when, on reasonable judgment, it is not an extension of the program's own domain; a form that the library has for one number type, rank or sibling trait and lacks for another is the plainest case. Whoever writes it there first studies how the library does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern, such as its `excludes` clauses. This rule governs how the library is extended; it does not choose between two of the team's designs of the language (P-26).
- P-28 **Fleshing out the standard library is a very important task.** Its next layer is algebra: traits such as `Ring` and `Field`, which the library does not declare yet, and what machine learning's matrices and tensors need, so that the library's algebraic traits, such as `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`, reach them too. Why: the curator wants those matrices and tensors to have the mathematical rigour that the library's way of building its types promises. The work edits the standard library itself, in `Library/`, not a separate tree of the revival's own outside it (P-27, how the library is extended). It is parked off the path to microGPT compiled. Two matrix ideas of his wait beside it: square matrices of one size as a multiplicative ring, and diagonal matrices of one size as a ring whose product commutes.
- P-29 **Walk's speed is irrelevant to every judgement of Fortress's performance.** Walk is far slower than Python's interpreter (`explorations/microgpt-port.md`, "Step-0 results", a measurement of 2026-08-23). Fortress's performance is judged on the compiled path, once the compiler runs programs. So no performance decision rests on walk's timings. In particular, until microGPT runs compiled, C4, the flat microGPT program, is not edited for speed. The gate never runs microGPT's two programs, C4 and the APL-style program, because they run too long to be tests. Why: walk is the unoptimised path, as a debug build is in Swift, where performance is not judged either.
- P-30 **The check of microGPT under walk after a batch must take less than a minute.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. The minute is the curator's goal, for a check that runs only about two forward-and-backward passes of the model, not a full training, and compares the results with reference values. That is enough to show that the model's mathematics still works, and that the library's changes, such as those to the arrays, did not break it. A slower check is to him a waste of time. The commit stage of each batch, the step that lands its changes, runs the check as `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh`, the quick versions of microGPT's two programs at once, outside the gate.
- P-32 **The record's maps are kept current and used, so that nothing that the record holds is worked out again from scratch.** The maps are `FACTS.md`, `INDEX.md` and the territory map, `explorations/coordinator/map/`. The territory map surveys the repository down to where the team wrote the intent of each design. Part of that intent is written only in the papers under `Papers/`, not in the specification. So the map covers the papers too, and shows where to look up a design's intent. `INDEX.md` is read whole at the coordinator's boot, at the start of each session and after each compaction, and each worker's brief carries a mission briefing from the territory map, not the whole map. The territory map's surveys date from 2026-09-16 (its README), so a status or a line number in them can be stale.
- P-33 **The work toward microGPT compiled follows the phases, in the order that the curator approved.** These phases are steps of the work, not the compiler's phases, and they are numbered 3 to 6, after two earlier ones. Phase 3 ends when the compiled checker reports no error on the apis and components of the interpreter's library that the distance to the switch-over counts (F-53 defines the distance, says what it counts and holds its value). The library's other components are not part of phase 3: each is cleared before the first program that needs it, and at the latest before walk runs the checker (P-12), so `System` by the switch-over, since the compiler's tests need it (F-293); F-290 counts their errors. Phase 4, the switch-over: first the natives, the library's `builtinPrimitive` bindings made to run on the compiled path, then the compiled path reads the interpreter's library and the compiler's prelude is deleted; phase 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code generator's open gaps; phase 6, microGPT runs fast. Code-generator work goes on beside that order, under either library (P-37). Row 320, an api implemented by a component of another name does not link, is part of the switch-over's design.

### The one library and the compiled checker

- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. Why: the switch-over spares porting the interpreter's library into the compiler's; the revival develops the checker until it accepts that fuller library. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled; F-293 holds the compiler's fourth file, `CompilerSystem`). The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library takes a design of the prelude's where it is the team's later decision, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library.
- P-38 **The compiler prelude's own text is not repaired: its defects go with it at the switch-over.** A helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is fixed for the one library, and the prelude's value moves with it (F-313). Its `Maybe` block and its `REM` guard `if other = -1 then 0` stay as landed until the prelude is deleted, and their tests stay. Then the compiled tests respell its reversed wrapping and saturating operators (row 348), `ZZ64`'s compiled shift closes (row 381), and the specification's `shift` reaches the compiled path (row 383). `XXXShiftDeclRungI` is then promoted, and the switch-over batch finds the compiler tests that bind `shift`, a reserved name from then on.
- P-39 **Every batch's gate measures the checker count, and its total never turns the gate red.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. Its gate runs the gate's steps on their merged tree, and then the checker count, as step 8 (`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`); the gate of `fortress-repo`'s gate part has no such step. The checker count and the distance to the switch-over both count the compiled checker's errors on the interpreter's library. The count stops where the checker crashes or meets an error that it cannot get past; the distance counts every error, over all apis and components (F-53 defines both and holds their values). A rise of the count's total is reported and never fails a batch on its own. The count's stage can still turn the gate red on the faults that F-66 names. One is a checker crash that no rung of the batch listed in advance as expected, in the field `expectedCheckerCrash` of the batch's manifest, the part of the batch's script that declares each rung's task. Until the switch-over lands, every batch's gate also measures the distance, in a stage that only reports. Why: the count checks only the `FortressLibrary` component (F-53), so a native binding moved onto a helper in another component is checked by the distance alone, and P-58 has each moved binding checked from the step that moves it.
- P-40 **Sizes are checked, and a size that inference leaves unknown is an error only where it is used.** A size is a `nat` or `int` static parameter, such as the length of an array in its type. The compiled checker checks sizes, and refuses a size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` (F-140, the bound on both paths). Wherever the array design, the compiled path's design for arrays (P-85), creates a JVM array, it checks the length there, at run time, and refuses one over 2^31-1. A size that inference leaves unknown is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value. So a declaration may declare a size that none of its types uses, and pass. A call that cannot fix a size of the declaration that it would choose is refused, also inside an overload set, instead of passing over that declaration. In the rule that no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait, two instantiations differ when any static argument but an operator differs, so `Vec[\3\]` and `Vec[\4\]` are two; boolean arguments count too once the checker has boolean parameters. A size used as a number, as in the range `0#n`, converts to `ZZ32` where one is needed, as a numeral does. The 17 vector and matrix operators of the `FortressLibrary` api declare only the sizes that their types use, the change of `explorations/perf-probes/array-sites/e3-rebased.patch`. It finishes the team's own fix of 2008, which removed those sizes from the component only. The JVM length check waits for the array design; under walk such an array dies with a raw Java exception (row 527). The checker still passes over a declaration whose unfixed size occurs in its own parameter type (row 400). The checker compares no boolean arguments (row 406).
- P-41 **On the compiled path, a size static argument travels at run time as a descriptor object, as a type argument does.** A generic type's descriptor has a field for each of its static parameters that is not an operator. The team's code generator already emitted that field for a size, with nothing to put in it, and the size's descriptor fills it. Each size value, such as the 3 of `Vec[\3\]`, has one descriptor, which `RTTIsize.of` takes from a table; no Java class is written for it. This is the team's pattern for instantiating types, applied to numbers. An operator static argument, by contrast, stays a name known only at compile time (F-39, how both paths carry it). The curator sees no need for an operator argument to be carried at run time the way types and sizes are. F-129 holds what runs and its open rows.
- P-42 **A type parameter declared without a bound has the implicit bound `Any`, not `Object`.** `Any` holds tuples, functions and `()`, which `Object` does not. The library instantiates its generic containers at tuple types: its arrays indexed by pairs, such as `(ZZ32,ZZ32)`, are among them. The specification states the bound `Any`, with a callout that records that the Working Draft of February 2011 said `Object`.
- P-43 **The exclusion rule stays, and the number tower is flat (route A).** The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule. So the library's numbers are flat, as the team (Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen) flattened the compiler prelude in 2009 and 2010. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`, each with its own algebra, and `Number` has no catch-all operators. Why: the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way, and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule. He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen. F-46 prices a return to route C.
- P-44 **`AnyIntegral` stays closed by its `comprises` clause, and the compiled checker reads the clause as the team's 2012 texts do.** The library's `AnyIntegral`, whose `comprises` clause lists the five integer types `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64`, stays closed. Beside the clause stays a comment in the team's `NOT YET` form, by which the team's library records a clause that it cannot write yet: here `comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I\]`. The `where` form is built (P-151), but neither path takes this clause yet: the front end of both paths refuses it on a trait that declares a coercion (row 831), and walk refuses the library at load with it (row 804). `Integral[\I\]` extends `AnyIntegral` and is not in the list. The checker accepts such a generic trait below a closed trait when every type that the checker knows below it is listed. The clause's text in the library, and walk, stay as they are. Why: the team's 2012 texts, Luchangco's Types chapter and Welterweight, are its later word (P-25), and by them the clause is right as written. The rule leaves a hole that every way of closing `AnyIntegral` shares, except the team's 2008 way, a `comprises` clause on `Integral[\I\]` itself: a program's own subtype of `Integral`, declared in another component, is accepted although no listed type is above it. Row 487 records the hole, and this decision does not close it.
- P-45 **Overloaded declarations may differ in their static parameters.** The specification drops its sentence that forbids this, and keeps it as superseded text. It states instead the overloading model of the type group's 2011 paper (`Papers/Types/`), which the compiled checker already used. The checker keeps the paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type. It checks the Return Type Rule over every instance of a generic declaration that the argument types allow, not over one guessed instance. One rule of the old sentence survives: if one generic declaration is more specific than another, their static parameters must line up position by position, as Java's rule for overriding a generic method requires. The compiled checker tests it only where the two declarations have as many static parameters of their own (F-75). Walk chooses among overloads by the parameter types that each declaration declares, not by the order in which they are written. At load, walk judges each pair of two generic declarations by the checker's rules on their declared parameter types. It does not refuse a pair only because none of their parameter types exclude, as when one declaration is more specific than the other. Walk and the checker must accept the same pairs. The library repairs, by declarations of its own, the overload sets that the checker refused, and no line of microGPT's two programs changes. Where walk or the checker still judges a pair against these rules: walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on the instance that a call makes (F-26); both paths refuse the paper's own valid example (row 539); walk refuses two generic functional methods of a trait without static parameters whose declared domains lie one inside the other, and fails at a call on such a pair in a generic trait (rows 779 and 780); and walk and the checker disagree on three kinds of pair (rows 786 to 788).
- P-46 **A conversion only makes a call possible: it never changes which declaration runs when one already fits.** The declaration that runs is chosen on the parameter types that each overload declares: first those that apply, then the most specific of them (P-45). A generic declaration applies if some type within its bounds takes the arguments. Only then is the chosen declaration instantiated by promotion: at the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce (P-74). So beside `op(a: Any, b: Any)`, `op[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T)` applies to a call with a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64`, at `T = Number`. It is the more specific, so it runs, at `ZZ64`. Why: the curator wants fast generic code that a JVM can specialise. His own broader rule is not taken: to apply any conversion that reaches a specific declaration, and to fall back to a plain one only when none does. Walk and the compiled checker both infer static arguments with coercion, by the same promotion. The compiled path inserts the conversions statically. P-49 gives the order in which the checker tries a call. Row 537: the compiled dispatch between two generic declarations of one name with different bounds.
- P-47 **Each integer type declares its own `MIN`, `MAX` and `MINMAX`, instead of relying on those that it inherits from the generic order traits.** The integer types are the five that `AnyIntegral` lists: `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64`. Through `Integral`, each inherits the three operators from `StandardTotalOrder` and the `StandardMin`, `StandardMax` and `StandardMinMax` that it extends. `a MINMAX b` is the pair `(a MIN b, a MAX b)`. The `MAX` that a `ZZ64` inherits types `self` as the order trait, so neither it nor `QQ`'s `MAX` is more specific. Under walk, `b MAX 1` for a `ZZ64` `b` would then stop the run with "Ambiguous coercion". With their own declarations, these operators answer at the type that their arguments promote to (P-74), as `b + 1` does. Why: it is the library's own device. `QQ`, `RR64` and the compiler's prelude declare all three, and the specification's `ZZ` declares its own `MIN` and `MAX`.
- P-48 **A type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes its bound, never `Bottom`.** The arguments leave a parameter unfixed when it occurs only in the result type; when two arguments meet at it with no narrowest type into which both convert (a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` have one, `ZZ64`, by P-74); or when dispatch, at run time, picks a generic declaration and must choose the instance to run. Its instance is then the intersection of its upper bounds (`Any` if it has none). At checking, that is narrowed by what the call's expected type (P-49 defines it) requires of the declared return type; at run time, by the static type that the checker gave the call. 102	### Arrays and the model program
103	
104	- P-84 **On the compiled path, the array of every number type is to be stored unboxed, in a Java array of its primitive type, and every array is to have the most efficient store that its element type allows; arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** `RR64` goes in a `double[]`, `ZZ32` in an `int[]`, and so on, for each number type that has a Java primitive type; `RR64`'s `double[]`, the model's, is the first case. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected. 112	### The specification's revision
113	
114	- P-95 **Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason.** When the revival changes the language, it updates `Specification/` with the change, so that the text and the implementation do not disagree. The original text and the reasoning are kept, so that route C stays open. Route C is the design that P-43 set aside: a nested number tower, under the forest rule of the team's 2012 patent applications (F-46 gives what a return to it would need). 115	- P-96 **A change of the specification is shown in layers, as the team showed its own changes in the 1.0 release of 2008 and in the working draft of 2009.** This form is the revision form. A callout that prints in every build marks each changed passage; a `\note` will not do, since a release build hides it. Appendix I's revival section has an entry for each change: its reason, its original text, what a return to route C would mean for it, or that it would be the same under route C (P-95 says what route C is), and the decision that it follows. The front matter has one paragraph on the revision, and a document in the repository holds the full reasoning. Citations call the unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, the Working Draft of February 2011: the copy is that draft byte for byte, and only its `fortress.1.0.pdf` is the 1.0 release (F-163). The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/specification.md` gives each part in full, including what else an Appendix I entry holds.
116	- P-97 **The specification's examples that break the exclusion rule take the library's shapes, and each original stays, marked "Not allowed".** The Working Draft offered such examples as legal. Each now shows the shape that the library uses for the same thing, with the original beside it under the specification's own mark, "Not allowed". The specification states the rule, which it calls instantiation exclusion, once, in the two parts of Luchangco's Types chapter of 2012 (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`; P-25): `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` says which instantiations exclude each other, and `basic/traits.tex` says that a declaration may not extend two that do. The covariance example, a trait that extends other instantiations of itself, is rewritten and marked in the same way. Its callout adds one sentence: the type group's later design, in the same Types chapter, declares variance with a `covariant` modifier, which neither walk nor the compiled path implements (row 404 records the gap). The calculi of Appendix A keep their rules as the team wrote them, under a callout that they predate the rule.
117	- P-98 **`TotalComparison` extends `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]`, so that the library's `BIG MIN` and `BIG MAX` work over total comparisons.** It does so in the library's api and component, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `.fss`. Why: it is the library's own device, which its other ordered types use. The curator took it on the coordinator's recommendation. It stands and blocks no work.
118	
119	### The suites and the gate
120	
121	- P-102 **Test first, the test kept.** Every edit of source code in the original tree starts from a failing test. The worker adds the test to the test suite, sees it fail, makes the fix, and sees it pass. The test then stays in the suite for good. An edit of the specification or of documentation is not source code and needs no test. The gate's three test runs, `ant testFast`, `ant testSystem` and `ant testSpecData` (P-124), must pass when the work lands; they need not pass after every edit. The test and the fix may land in one commit. Why: the rule replaces one-off validation scripts, which no later build runs. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/tests-writing.md` says how to write the test.
122	- P-103 **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test's result is pass or fail, as the team designed the suites. A value that matters is checked inside the test, with the checks that the harness already has: an `assert` call in an interpreter test, a `run_out_equals` key in a compiled test's `.test` file. What a test prints beyond its checks does not count. So no expected-output files are added. They are not proposed to the curator again, and neither is a comparison of what a test prints beyond its checks with an earlier run's output. Why: when the suite's designers let a test pass without a further check, what it prints need not be checked.
123	- P-124 **The specification's examples are a step of the gate, and every one must pass.** `ant testSpecData` runs the examples extracted from `Specification/` under walk (F-114 says which 130 it runs), and the gate fails if any of them fails. When an example fails, the implementation is fixed: the example is not respelled to get around a gap in walk, and no list of examples allowed to fail is kept.
124	- P-125 **The suites run Fortress in parallel, pinned at four threads in `build.xml`.** `build.xml` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS` to 4 for the two suites, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`, so that every run of them uses four threads, whatever the calling shell sets. A test that parallelism makes fail, on every run or only on some, is written wrong, for example a write that needs `atomic`, or it shows a defect. Either is fixed, never hidden by running at one thread. Why: Fortress is parallel by default, so a suite at one thread has a blind spot, and sparing the four-CPU machine is no reason for one.
125	- P-150 **No resident compiler is built.** A background JVM that serves Fortress commands, as Scala 2's `fsc` did, would save too little of the workers' time to be worth building (F-234), so the speed work goes to the checker itself (P-148). It is not tried again unless something significant changes.

### Numbers

- P-66 **The integer principle: Java's and the JVM's defaults stay where they make sense, and are corrected where they fail high performance or mathematical precision.** The team did so with rounding. A hardware behaviour that bytecode can express gets its own explicit spelling, as the specification's wrapping and saturating operators do. Where the JVM prevents a correct implementation, the project gives way for now. The peers to compare are Julia, X10, Swift and Rust.
- P-67 **`round` on an exact half goes to the even integer, on both paths.** Under walk and on the compiled path, `round(2.5)` gives 2: an `RR64` or `RR32` value rounds an exact half to the even integer, as a rational does. This is the specification's rule for rationals, the default rounding of IEEE 754, and the rule of the team's own `round` on rationals.
- P-68 **On the float types, `floor` and `ceiling` return the same float type, while the brackets ⌊x⌋ and ⌈x⌉, `round` and `truncate` return `ZZ`, the unbounded integer.** So `floor(2.5)` is the `RR64` value 2.0, and ⌊2.5⌋ is to be the `ZZ` value 2. Row 330: one library rung after the switch-over, which first counts the interpreter tests whose output changes, then makes the brackets, `round` and `truncate` return `ZZ` in each of the library's declarations of them; today `truncate` is `ZZ64` on both paths, the brackets are `ZZ64` under walk and `RR64` compiled, and `round` is `ZZ64`, but `ZZ` in the `FortressLibrary` component's `trait RR64`.

A count at or beyond the width gives 0, or -1 for `RSHIFT` of a negative value, and a negative count shifts the other way, as Swift's and Julia's shifts do. The count may have any integer type, and the shift works at the width of the value shifted. On `ZZ`, the unbounded integers ℤ, `shift(x, k)` is ⌊x·2^k⌋ at any count; there the specification defines `x LSHIFT k` as `shift(x, k)` and `x RSHIFT k` as `shift(x, -k)`. On the compiled path, a shift of a fixed-width value works on the JVM's `int` or `long`, never through `ZZ`. Why: a shift through `ZZ` costs speed wherever the JVM cannot remove it. Row 442: the compiled `NN32` and `NN64` shifts, refused today. Row 383: `ZZ`'s `shift`, which the compiler's prelude does not declare. Row 381: a count of another integer type, where the compiled path refuses a `ZZ`, `NN32` or `NN64` count and computes a `ZZ64` count on a `ZZ32` at 64 bits.

The rule applies on both paths. Why: the specification says that both results are nonnegative, and its general rule raises `IntegerOverflow` for an integer result that does not fit. The same general rule makes `GCD` raise it where the divisor does not fit, as in the specification's example `-2^31 GCD 0` on `ZZ32`. Row 442: `GCD` and `LCM` on the compiled path's `NN32` and `NN64`.
- P-71 **An overflow guard tests for the type's most negative value, not for `a = -a`, so `|0|`, `-0` and `0 DIV -1` do not overflow.** On a signed fixed-width type, only the most negative value overflows when it is negated, taken in absolute value or divided by -1. The test `a = -a` is true for that value, and also for 0. Walk already gave 0 in the three cases. On the compiled path, the natives of negation, absolute value and division on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` test for the most negative value. The same faulty test sat in `ZZ64`'s multiplication, through which its `REM`, `MOD`, `GCD` and `LCM` compute, so `0 · 5`, `3 REM 5` and `12 GCD 18` raised; that multiplication now raises only when the exact product does not fit. Why: no reading of the specification makes the three cases overflow.
- P-72 **`narrow` keeps the low 32 bits of a value that the narrower type cannot hold, signed and unsigned, on both paths, and raises no `IntegerOverflow`.** The decision covers `narrow` from a `ZZ64` to a `ZZ32` and from an `NN64` to an `NN32`. A value that the narrower type holds is unchanged; any other becomes the value of the narrower type with the same low 32 bits. Why: the team's specification said nothing on `narrow`, and the team's boundary test `ProjectFortress/tests/UnsignedTest.fss` asserts the low 32 bits for `NN64` values. On the unsigned types, keeping the low bits is a bit operation, like a shift, and the signed `narrow` gets the same answer.

So a subtraction below 0 on `NN32` raises. Climb batch 28 has landed. Its commit stage pushed `f56d6516` at 08:46 UTC (09:46 your time).

- **Result:** all seven rungs were approved (R only after a judge ruled), and the gate is green. microGPT's quick walk check passes 7 of 7 on both programs.
- **Measures:** the distance and the checker count are both 0. The checker now finishes its check of `value object Char`, so the two crash rows are gone.
- **Natives:** 52 of the library's 424 live bindings still name glue classes, down from 102.

What each rung did:
- **V:** builds the integer conversions you decided (P-161): checked `as…` getters, `bitsAs…` getters, and `ZZ`'s `narrow` and `widen` deleted.
- **R:** puts the reader side of the file streams, and `FileWriteStream`, on helpers (P-164).
- **A:** builds the arrays' store in your Q2 answer: an `Object[]` with the slot API in the compiled transaction (P-169).
- **K:** makes the checker order a call's candidates by a linear extension of their partial order (a total order consistent with the partial one), which fixes row 929.
- **H:** puts threads, `abort` and the task trace on runtime helpers.
- **S:** puts `System`'s natives on helpers, and builds `args` in Fortress per your Q3 answer, option 1 (P-170).
- **T:** fixes row 733: the code generator now compiles a type whose first supertrait is an imported api's trait.

The batch left 35 items for your review, all on PLAN's review list. The biggest ones:
- V added two Java helpers for `ZZ`, which goes against the plan's no-new-Java default.
- Walk's immutable arrays now ignore a second initialisation instead of overwriting.
- Two new compiled transaction defects: a livelock, and a nested `atomic` block's abort that the outer block's handler catches.

Next, with nothing needed from you:
1. The post-batch review is running.
2. Then the record-landing update.

After that, I'll put this morning's questions to you, one ask per message: the four on literals, and the one on walk's `Int` leak (row 364). The two reviews behind them are pushed:

- **Walk's immutable arrays** keep a first initialisation and lose their located error (splits 5 and 6).
- **`genZZ.perturb`** raises beyond `ZZ64` (split 2).
- **A tie's arrow** is the first minimal candidate, in an order that is not a property of the program (split 8).

D. PLAN's "Where we stand" and phase 4's lines (Part 4).

**Corrections of an entry's ground that change no decision, for the entries' histories:**
- F-240's distance figure, 205 s, was taken beside another agent's JVM as well as `testFast` (section 2).
- Climb batch 27's review counted 2.80M for climb batch 26's landing work; with `-home-user-fortress-landing-26` it is 3.40M (section 3).

**Confirmations:**
- The count's table equals climb batch 27's; the distance reads 0 with no crash, and `Char` is checked.

<!-- The record-landing workflow: after a climb batch's post-batch review, bring the record in line with the landing (FACTS, POSITIONS and their histories, the ledger rows the evidence names, PLAN, PLAN-history, the review queue, INDEX and line fixes in other notes) in a worktree of its own, land its two commits on `main` and run the orientation update after them; then have the skill writer bring the `fortress-repo` skill in line, a cold read, the writer's fixes, the page of the skill's changes and the pushes; then the revival page's update, its commit and push, and its republish; how to launch it, what it writes, and how the coordinator reviews the landed commits. -->

# The record-landing workflow

`record-landing.js` does the record's work after a landing, which the coordinator did by hand through a record writer and a routing worker until climb batch 24. It is the smallest first version of the design `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-landing-workflow.md` (`5384a4f35`), which the curator approved with its eight defaults on 2026-11-02. It runs in six stages for the record, in the pattern of the orientation workflow (`../orientation/orientation.js`), five more for the skill after the orientation update ("The skill update"), and one for the revival page ("The revival page"):

1. **Sort** (Opus, `sort.md`): `prepare.sh` makes the worktree and its branch and writes the evidence into the run's folder (`evidence.py`'s header lists its six files; `plan.md` ends with the PLAN lines that look stale, from `plan-moves.py --stale-at`, cut at 40,000 characters, past which the whole list is in `plan-stale.txt`, which the cut line names); the sorter reads it, the review's routing part and the batch record's items, and writes `owed.md`, one line per change with its number, its home, its kind, its weight, its ground and its writer, and marks each kind and each "Needed by" that no source states as set by the workflow.
2. **Write**: a Sonnet driver runs `drive.sh 1` in the background and waits for it in steps of 240 s, under the five minutes that its prompt cache lives. `drive.sh` starts two headless Opus writer streams side by side through the worktree's copy of `../record-clarity/writer-stream.sh`: the entries writer (`entries.md`: FACTS, POSITIONS, an entry's history, ledger rows, as `record.apply` and `rows.rewrite`) and the routing writer (`routing.md`: PLAN, PLAN-history, the queue, INDEX, other notes, edited in the worktree). Then `checks.sh 1` writes `mech-1.md`.
3. **Check**: the checker (`check.md`: coverage, fidelity, form and routing) and the clarity cold reader (`../record-clarity/coldread.md`, unchanged, told to write its report in parts of five entries) on `clean.txt`, side by side.
4. **Fix**: `drive.sh 2` resumes both streams once with the three reports, then `checks.sh 2` writes `mech-2.md`.
5. **Judge** (Opus, `judge.md`): apply or hold each change once, `final.apply` and `final.rewrite`, `diff.md` (within 10,000 characters), and `final.sh`, which runs every check again and makes two commits on the branch. The judge writes nothing after the commits.
6. **Land** (Sonnet, in the script): only when the judge's checks pass (the branch holds its commits past AT, `mech-final.md` says every check passes, the worktree is clean), the lander puts the two commits on `main`, runs the checks on `main`, pushes, and removes the worktree and the branch; then the script runs the orientation workflow in update mode as a child workflow (`../orientation/orientation.js`, one level deep), on the entries in the orientation call of `diff.md`'s "Next". "Landing its result" gives each step.
7. **Skills** (a Sonnet driver; the skill writer, a headless Opus session): `skills.sh N 1` writes the writer's task from `skill-task.md` and the landed files, and starts a fresh writer on it through `../skill-writer.sh new`; the writer installs what the orientation judge accepts and brings the `fortress-repo` skill in line with the landing, and commits on `main`.
8. **Cold read** (Opus): the changed parts, by `../../skill-cold-read-brief.md`, as a worker new to the repository.
9. **Fixes**: `skills.sh N 2` resumes the same writer on the cold read's flags (`skill-fixes.md`).
10. **Page** (Opus, `page.md`): the page of `fortress-repo`'s landed changes, by the source and the URL that the boot note names, published by that URL.
11. **Push** (Sonnet, in the script): `folders.sh N` commits the run's folders, then the pushes as the Land stage's; the result's `line` is the one line for the coordinator's chat message.
12. **Revival page** (Sonnet, in the script; then a Sonnet publisher, `revival-publish.md`): `../revival-page/update.py --landing N --run-start base` in the main tree, the files that it names committed by named paths and pushed as the Push stage's; then the page published by its URL with the Artifact tool. The result's `line` gains the page's commit and version.

The mechanical checks (`checks.sh`): the six record files reset to the worktree's base, the cut-only POSITIONS lines checked with `../record-clarity/words-subset.py --root`, the writers' files applied with `record.py apply`, `../ledger-clarity/apply.py` and `ledger.py add` (the new rows of `rows.add`, or at the final round the judge's `final.add` where it wrote one), each history block "by climb batch N landing workflow (Opus)"; then `record.py check --base`, `ledger.py check`, `ledger.py landing-check`, `check-index.sh`, `plan-moves.py`, `queue-check.py` and `lengths.py`.

- `plan-moves.py` fails a line out of PLAN that is not word for word in PLAN-history. Its `LOOK` lines, which never fail, name each PLAN line that still looks stale: a line whose own review-queue item is in (a) and that carries no cleanup's mark ("closed at the cleanup of DATE"), a list of items that names a settled one or differs from the queue's list that it names, and a review finding that a commit outside the record names. The checker takes each as a coverage failure, unless `owed.md` or the routing report says why the line stays.
- `queue-check.py` fails a gap in the new numbers, a new open item without "Needed by", a count that its items do not make, and an item new in "Answered by a decision of his" that cites no word of his on that same item, or that names a default taken without him ("at its default", "by the coordinator"). Such an item stays open, landed and then reviewed. The rule leans to keeping an item open: a true answer of his worded with those phrases fails too, and is reworded.
- `lengths.py` informs: each changed entry's length, and each entry already over 600 that grew, which the judge holds unless the owed clause alone explains the growth.

`drive.sh --dry-run` prints the commands of a round and starts nothing. The streams' headless sessions run `facts-extract.sh` and the `git` reads that `writer-stream.sh` allows, and not `record.py`, `ledger.py` or the checks, which need an approval that a headless session cannot get. So `checks.sh` is the first to apply and check the writers' files, after each round, and the fix round reads its output in `mech-1.md`.

Every brief reads the record only through `facts-extract.sh`, `record.py` and `ledger.py` in the worktree, and entries are written only through `record.py`. The run takes three arguments and no text, so a run gives the workflow data, never rules of its own. The briefs change only at the curator's yes.

## Running it

After the post-batch review is committed:

    Workflow({ scriptPath: '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/record-landing.js',
               args: { batch: 'N', base: 'BASE', landing: 'LANDING' } })

It makes `/home/user/fortress-landing-N` on the branch `record/landing-N` at `main`'s head. A replay adds `at`, the commit to make the worktree at, and its worktree and branch end in `-replay`; it stops after the judge, and lands nothing and runs neither the orientation update, the skill update nor the revival page. The replay of climb batch 24's landing, before the first live run at climb batch 25's:

    Workflow({ scriptPath: '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/record-landing.js',
               args: { batch: '24', base: 'b0f6cd6b7', landing: '25238e60c', at: '43cd61b62' } })

That one runs in `/home/user/fortress-landing-24-replay` on `record/landing-24-replay`. A killed run resumes with the same script path, `resumeFromRunId` and the same args, byte for byte; each script skips a step whose output exists. During a run the coordinator writes none of the files that the workflow writes; a decision that the curator gives meanwhile is recorded after the landing. The design's estimate for a landing like climb batch 24's was 0.9M to 1.7M tokens written and 1 to 1.5 hours; the replay wrote 2.06M in 65 minutes (`process-engineering/record-landing-replay-24.md`, section 6). With the driver's waits under five minutes and the cold read in parts, a like landing writes about 1.8M, an estimate. The skill update adds about 0.4M to 0.7M, an estimate: at climb batch 25's landing the coordinator's two writer tasks wrote 107K to the cache, the rest is the cold read, the page and

## What it writes

Until the landing, everything goes in the worktree, and the main tree is not touched. The run's folder, `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/record-landing/` in the worktree, holds `run.env`, the evidence, `owed.md`, the writers' files, briefs and reports (the entries writer's new ledger rows in `rows.add`: each row line, `| ? | ...`, under a line `## TITLE` that names its section, a title of `ledger.py sections`, as in `## 10. Strings, maps and printing`; `checks.sh` adds each with `ledger.py add` after the other applies, so the first commit carries it, and names in its summary a row line with no such line above it, which it does not add), `check.md`, `cold-read.md`, `mech-1.md`, `mech-2.md`, `mech-final.md`, `final.apply`, `final.rewrite`, the commit messages and `diff.md`, and the logs of the rounds, which git ignores. The markers of finished rounds are in the worktree's `tmp/re

## Landing its result

The workflow lands its own result, by the curator's rule of 2026-11-03 (`../../HELD.md`, "Held in chat (2026-11-03)", 06:2x); the design's decision 6, the coordinator's cherry-pick, is reversed. After the judge, the lander, in the main tree:

1. Checks the judge's checks: the branch holds its commits past AT, `mech-final.md` says "Every check passes.", the worktree is clean. If one fails, it lands nothing, and the result's `stopped` says so; the worktree and the branch stay.
2. Puts the commits on `main`: `git merge --ff-only` of the branch when `main` is still at AT, which keeps the judge's hashes; otherwise `git cherry-pick AT..BRANCH`, since `main` moved during the run. A refusal or a conflict is aborted, `main` stays where it was, and the run stops as in step 1.
3. Runs on `main` `record.py check --base <main before the landing>`, `ledger.py landing-check <the batch's base>` and `check-index.sh`. If one fails, `git reset --keep` takes the run's commits off the local `main`, which is not pushed, and the run stops as in step 1.
4. Pushes, in the order of the `fortress-repo` skill's committing part: `git log origin/main..main` lists only the run's commits, then `main`, `main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8` and `main:blinded-fable`. A refused push, or another agent's commit in that list, stops the run, landed but not all pushed, before the orientation update.
5. `git worktree remove` the worktree, without `--force`, and `git branch -D` the branch.
6. Reads the facts list of the orientation call in the landed `diff.md`'s "Next" (the entries that the landing and the run added or changed); the script then runs `orientation.js` with `mode: 'update'`, `out` the batch's `climb-batch-N/orientation/` and `stream` `orientation-bN`. Nothing waits on the coordinator between the record's commits and the update. With no entry there, the update is skipped, and the skill update still runs. If the update fails to start, the run stops, landed and pushed, before the skill update. The skill update below installs its result.

The coordinator then reviews the commits on `main`: `git show --stat` of each commit the result's `land` names, and the landed `diff.md`, not the record. It asks whether it would have done anything differently, and names each POSITIONS change to the curator, from `diff.md`, as the `coordinator` skill's "Quiet times" says. Each held change: run it again, file it in the queue, or leave it.
